title: Question 4 (Page 67, #56)
question:
The diagram shows an experimental set-up to study how transpiration rate varies when a leafy shoot was exposed to different environmental conditions. Four such experiments, 1, 2, 3 and 4, were set up and the set-ups were placed at four different locations: in the centre of a grass field, under a large shady tree, in an enclosed cupboard, on a windy open hilltop. The distance travelled by the air bubble in the capillary tube was measured over four hours in the day time and the results are shown in the following table. Which row correctly shows where each experimental set-up was placed?

&&img&& PAGE_67_Q56 &&img&&
explanation: The set-up placed on the windy hilltop showed the greatest rate of transpiration (and therefore the greatest distance moved by the air bubble) as the wind blew away the shell of humidity that built up around the leafy shoot. This would maintain a steep concentration gradient for the diffusion of water vapour out of the stomata on the leaves. Being placed on a hilltop meant that the leafy shoot would be exposed to similar environmental conditions as that placed in the open grass field, except that the wind would cause a higher rate of transpiration from the leafy shoot on the hilltop. Both the set-ups in the grass field and on the hilltop would experience relatively higher temperatures and higher exposure to light. This would result in a higher rate of transpiration in general. The set-up placed under the tree would experience a lower temperature and less exposure to light, hence, the rate of transpiration would be lower as the stomata in the leaves would have a smaller pore size compared to those placed in the grass field and on top of the hilltop. The set-up placed in the enclosed cupboard would show the lowest rate of transpiration as the humidity would be higher in the cupboard, decreasing the rate of diffusion of water vapour from the leafy shoot. The absence of light would also cause the guard cells to be flaccid and hence the smaller stomatal pores.

options.option_text: grass field: 1, shady tree: 3, enclosed cupboard: 2, hilltop: 4
grass field: 2, shady tree: 4, enclosed cupboard: 3, hilltop: 1
grass field: 2, shady tree: 1, enclosed cupboard: 3, hilltop: 4
grass field: 4, shady tree: 1, enclosed cupboard: 2, hilltop: 3

title: Question 1 (Page 68, #1)
question:
Which blood vessels contain oxygenated blood?

&&img&& PAGE_68_Q1 &&img&&
explanation: The lungs allow diffusion of oxygen from the lungs into the blood capillaries, which will converge to form venules, and these venules subsequently converge to form the pulmonary vein (vessel 2) leading to the heart. The heart pumps out oxygenated blood via the aorta (vessel 4) to the rest of the body.

title: Question 2 (Page 68, #2)
question:
The direction of blood flow in one of the blood vessels is incorrect. Identify the blood vessel.

&&img&& PAGE_68_Q2 &&img&&
explanation: Vessel 6 is the hepatic portal vein that brings blood from the ileum directly to the liver.

title: Question 3 (Page 68, #3)
question:
Identify blood vessels 1, 3, 5 and 8.

&&img&& PAGE_68_Q3 &&img&&
explanation: Blood vessel 1 transports blood away from the heart, so it is a type of artery. Since vessel 1 is transporting blood away from the heart towards the lungs, it will be the pulmonary artery. Blood vessel 3 is a main blood vessel transporting blood from various organs in the body towards the heart, so it is the vena cava. Blood vessels associated with the liver are identified to be 'hepatic'. Since vessel 5 transports blood away from the liver, it is therefore the hepatic vein. Blood vessels associated with the kidney are identified to be 'renal'. Since vessel 8 transports blood towards the kidney, it is the renal artery.

options.option_text: vessel 1: hepatic vein, vessel 3: coronary vein, vessel 5: renal vein, vessel 8: pulmonary artery
vessel 1: pulmonary artery, vessel 3: inferior vena cava, vessel 5: hepatic vein, vessel 8: renal artery
vessel 1: renal vein, vessel 3: aorta, vessel 5: coronary artery, vessel 8: aorta
vessel 1: inferior vena cava, vessel 3: pulmonary vein, vessel 5: hepatic vein, vessel 8: renal artery

title: Question 4 (Page 68, #4)
question:
A blood sample is taken from one of the blood vessels and analysed for its constituents. The table shows the results of the analysis. Suggest the identity of the blood vessel that the blood sample is taken from.

&&img&& PAGE_68_Q4 &&img&&
explanation: Vessel 7 is the renal vein that is responsible for bringing deoxygenated blood from the kidney to the heart, hence, oxygen concentration would be low. Most of the amino acids in the blood would have been absorbed by the kidney and other organs, hence, resulting in low amino acid concentration. Since the kidney's function is to remove urea from the blood, the urea concentration would be very low in the renal vein.

title: Question 5 (Page 68, #5)
question:
The table shows the difference among three blood vessels X, Y and Z commonly found in the body. Based on the information given in the table above, what are the identities of vessels X, Y and Z?

&&img&& PAGE_68_Q5 &&img&&
explanation: Only veins contain valves, hence X must be a vein. Y has the smallest lumen of the three vessels and does not have a muscle layer, hence is a capillary.

options.option_text: vessel X: artery, vessel Y: capillary, vessel Z: vein
vessel X: capillary, vessel Y: vein, vessel Z: artery
vessel X: vein, vessel Y: artery, vessel Z: capillary
vessel X: vein, vessel Y: capillary, vessel Z: artery

title: Question 6 (Page 68, #6)
question: In which component of the blood is the transport of amino acids around the body is mainly found?
explanation: The plasma constitutes approximately 55% of the total blood volume and acts as a solvent for most water-soluble nutrients such as amino acids to be transported in the blood.

title: Question 1 (Page 69, #7)
question:
Which shows the correct functions of the different components of blood?

&&img&& PAGE_69_Q7 &&img&&
explanation: Platelets enable the formation of fibrin, which helps blood clot to minimise blood loss from damaged blood vessels.

options.option_text: plasma - transport oxygen in the blood
red blood cells - transport carbon dioxide in the blood
white blood cells - transport glucose in the blood

title: Question 2 (Page 69, #8)
question:
Which of the following components is likely to contain the soluble proteins such as fibrinogen, prothrombin and antibodies?

&&img&& PAGE_69_Q8 &&img&&
explanation: Most of the soluble proteins such as fibrinogen, prothrombin and antibodies are found in the blood plasma. Since the blood plasma is the least dense and the most plentiful of all the blood components, it must be component X.

title: Question 3 (Page 69, #9)
question:
Which of the following is present in largest quantities in component X?

&&img&& PAGE_69_Q9 &&img&&
explanation: Blood plasma, X, consists of mostly water, which acts as a solvent to dissolve various substances.

title: Question 4 (Page 69, #10)
question:
What are the identities of blood vessels X and Y?

&&img&& PAGE_69_Q10 &&img&&
explanation: Vessel X transports blood away from the lungs towards the heart, so it is the pulmonary vein. Vessel Y transports blood away from the heart towards body organs, so it is the aorta.

options.option_text: X: pulmonary artery, Y: vena cava
X: vena cava, Y: pulmonary artery

title: Question 5 (Page 69, #11)
question:
What is the identity and level of organisation of the structure labelled P?

&&img&& PAGE_69_Q11 &&img&&
explanation: From the diagram above, the capillary is made of similar endothelial cells forming a one-cell-thick capillary wall, hence, it is considered a tissue instead of an organ.

options.option_text: identity: artery, level of organisation: organ
identity: capillary, level of organisation: organ
identity: capillary, level of organisation: tissue
identity: vein, level of organisation: tissue

title: Question 1 (Page 70, #12)
question: Which of the following statements about capillaries is incorrect?
explanation: Capillaries do not have elastic tissues or muscular walls, unlike veins and arteries.

options.option_text: Capillaries carry blood from the arterioles to the venules.
Capillaries contain elastic tissue to withstand the high pressure in the blood.
Capillaries form dense networks within organs to enable efficient transport of nutrients.
Capillaries have a one-cell-thick wall to facilitate efficient diffusion of substances.

title: Question 2 (Page 70, #13)
question: How many times does a molecule of urea pass through the heart from the moment it leaves the renal vein until it reaches the aorta in a human?
explanation: The circulatory system of a human is a double loop system where the substances from the renal vein gets transported to the heart and gets pumped to the lungs before re-entering the heart the second time and leaving the heart via the aorta.

title: Question 3 (Page 70, #14)
question: What is the role played by platelets in blood clotting?
explanation: Platelets produce the enzyme thrombokinase that converts the protein prothrombin into thrombin. Platelets do not produce prothrombin. Fibrinogen is converted into fibrin by the enzyme thrombin, and not platelets.

options.option_text: to break down insoluble fibrin threads

title: Question 4 (Page 70, #15)
question:
The diagram simulates the circulatory system of a human. Identify pumps X and Y and blood vessels P and Q.

&&img&& PAGE_70_Q15 &&img&&
explanation: Pump X pumps oxygenated blood from the heart to other organs, hence should be the left ventricle. Pump Y pumps deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs, hence should be the right ventricle. Blood vessel P is the pulmonary vein, which brings oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium of the heart. Blood vessel Q is the vena cava, which brings deoxygenated blood from other organs back to the right atrium of the heart.

options.option_text: X: left atrium, Y: right atrium, P: aorta, Q: vena cava
X: right atrium, Y: left atrium, P: vena cava, Q: aorta
X: left ventricle, Y: right ventricle, P: pulmonary vein, Q: vena cava
X: right ventricle, Y: left ventricle, P: pulmonary artery, Q: aorta

title: Question 5 (Page 70, #16)
question:
The diagram shows different components of the blood as seen under light microscopy. Which component produces antibodies?

&&img&& PAGE_70_Q16 &&img&&
explanation: Lymphocytes produce antibodies. They can be recognised by their large nucleus that covers majority of the cell.

title: Question 6 (Page 70, #17)
question:
Identify process G and the substances that are exiting the capillary.

&&img&& PAGE_70_Q17 &&img&&
explanation: Useful substances such as oxygen and glucose diffuse out of the capillary into the liver cells.

options.option_text: process G: diffusion, substances exiting capillary: urea and carbon dioxide
process G: diffusion, substances exiting capillary: oxygen and glucose
process G: osmosis, substances exiting capillary: water and glucose
process G: osmosis, substances exiting capillary: water and urea

title: Question 7 (Page 70, #18)
question:
Liquid H is a fluid that surrounds the cells in the liver. Suggest the name given for H.

&&img&& PAGE_70_Q18 &&img&&
explanation: The fluid found around cells is known as tissue fluid.

title: Question 1 (Page 71, #19)
question:
Identify the fluid found in regions X and Y.

&&img&& PAGE_71_Q19 &&img&&
explanation: Blood plasma is the fluid found within the capillaries while the fluid found between the cells of the body is known as the tissue fluid.

options.option_text: X: blood plasma, Y: tissue fluid
X: tissue fluid, Y: blood plasma

title: Question 2 (Page 71, #20)
question:
How does fluid X differ from fluid Y in terms of composition?

&&img&& PAGE_71_Q20 &&img&&
explanation: Blood plasma proteins are too large to diffuse out of the plasma (X) into the tissue fluid (Y). Both X and Y contain glucose and urea. While blood cells can also freely move between fluid X and Y.

options.option_text: Fluid X contains glucose but fluid Y does not.
Fluid X contains plasma proteins but fluid Y does not.
Fluid X contains white blood cells but fluid Y does not.
Fluid Y contains urea but fluid X does not.

title: Question 3 (Page 71, #21)
question:
A drop of blood was placed under a light microscope and examined. The diagram shows the different components of blood. What are the names of structures X, Y and Z?

&&img&& PAGE_71_Q21 &&img&&
explanation: Red blood cells are characterised by their circular, biconcave shape. Lymphocytes have large, kidney-shaped nucleus while phagocytes tend to have irregular, lobed nucleus. Hence, Y must be a phagocyte. Z, the platelets are fragments of cells that are responsible for the clotting of blood.

options.option_text: X: lymphocyte, Y: platelets, Z: red blood cell
X: phagocyte, Y: red blood cell, Z: lymphocyte
X: red blood cell, Y: lymphocyte, Z: platelet
X: red blood cell, Y: phagocyte, Z: platelet

title: Question 4 (Page 71, #22)
question: An accident victim with blood type B required emergency blood transfusion upon admission to the trauma centre. Which of these donor blood groups would not be suitable for this blood transfusion?
explanation: The patient with blood type B would have anti-A antibodies in his blood plasma, hence, there will be serious/fatal agglutination of blood if the patient's blood came into contact with any donor blood that has antigen A on the red blood cells. Since blood group A and AB both have antigen A, these blood groups will not be suitable for the patient.

title: Question 5 (Page 71, #23)
question: Which of the following blood transfusion can be carried out safely?
explanation: Blood group O is the universal donor as the red blood cells contain neither antigen A nor antigen B on their surface, and hence, will not lead to agglutination regardless of the type of antibodies (a or b) found in the recipient's serum.

options.option_text: recipient blood group A, donor blood group B
recipient blood group AB, donor blood group O
recipient blood group B, donor blood group AB
recipient blood group O, donor blood group A

title: Question 6 (Page 71, #24)
question:
The diagram shows a cross-section of a human heart. X, Y and Z are three valves found in different regions of the heart. What are the identities of valves X, Y and Z?

&&img&& PAGE_71_Q24 &&img&&
explanation: Valve X is the atrio-ventricular valve on the right side of the heart, so it is the tricuspid valve. Valve Y is the valve found on the aorta, so it is the semi-lunar valve, preventing backflow of blood from the aorta to the left ventricle. Valve Z is the atrio-ventricular valve on the left side of the heart, so it is the bicuspid (or mitral) valve.

options.option_text: valve X: bicuspid, valve Y: tricuspid, valve Z: semi-lunar
valve X: bicuspid, valve Y: semi-lunar, valve Z: tricuspid
valve X: tricuspid, valve Y: semi-lunar, valve Z: bicuspid
valve X: semi-lunar, valve Y: bicuspid, valve Z: tricuspid

title: Question 7 (Page 71, #25)
question: Which of the following will not occur during ventricular diastole?
explanation: During ventricular diastole, the ventricular walls relax, causing the pressure of the aorta and pulmonary artery to be higher than that of the ventricles. This forces the semi-lunar valves shut.

options.option_text: blood pressure in the ventricle decreases

title: Question 1 (Page 72, #26)
question:
Identify blood vessel X.

&&img&& PAGE_72_Q26 &&img&&
explanation: The coronary artery branches out from the aorta and is responsible for transporting oxygenated blood to the heart muscle tissues.

title: Question 2 (Page 72, #27)
question: Fatty substances such as cholesterol and saturated fats may be deposited in the inner surface of blood vessel X, leading to a condition known as atherosclerosis. Which of the following factors does not increase the risk of atherosclerosis?
explanation: The factors increasing the risk of atherosclerosis are a diet high in cholesterol, stress (emotional, psychological and physical), as well as smoking. A high protein diet is not known to lead to atherosclerosis.

title: Question 3 (Page 72, #28)
question:
The diagram shows part of a capillary network surrounding tissues of an organ. At which point is the blood pressure the lowest?

&&img&& PAGE_72_Q28 &&img&&
explanation: The blood flows from a region of higher pressure to a region of lower pressure, hence D, being closest to the venule end will have the lowest pressure.

title: Question 4 (Page 72, #29)
question: Which of the following is not usually transported by the plasma?
explanation: Oxygen is usually transported by the red blood cells, not the plasma.

title: Question 5 (Page 72, #30)
question:
Which of the following blood vessels of the heart will become blocked due to excessive smoking?

&&img&& PAGE_72_Q30 &&img&&
explanation: Smoking would cause the coronary arteries (B) to be clogged up with fatty deposits, leading to coronary heart disease.

title: Question 6 (Page 72, #31)
question: Paul fasted for ten hours after having his breakfast. In which of the following blood vessels would the concentration of blood glucose be the highest?
explanation: After fasting for ten hours, the blood glucose level in the blood would be very low, even in the small intestine. The pancreas would secrete glucagon which would lead to the conversion of glycogen into glucose in the liver. The glucose released would leave the liver via the hepatic vein.

title: Question 7 (Page 72, #32)
question: A patient has haemophilia, a blood disorder that results in the inability of blood to clot properly. Which of the following proteins are likely to be lacking in the blood of this patient?
explanation: Thrombokinase is an essential enzyme in the blood clotting process in which it activates prothrombin into active thrombin enzymes, which in turn converts soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that enmesh the red blood cells forming clots.

title: Question 8 (Page 72, #33)
question:
The diagram shows the opening of the valve in a vein. Which statement correctly explains what causes the valve to open?

&&img&& PAGE_72_Q33 &&img&&
explanation: The opening or closing of valves is controlled by difference in the pressure between region X and region Y. The pressure in Y must be higher than that in X, allowing blood to flow through, and at the same time, keeping the valve open. Valves are designed to close shut when there is backflow of blood, hence A is incorrect.

options.option_text: The backflow of blood from Y to X causes the valve to open.
The blood pressure in X is higher than the blood pressure in Y, causing the valve to open.
The blood pressure in Y is higher than the blood pressure in X, causing the valve to open.
The layer of muscle around the vein relaxes and causes the valve to open.

title: Question 1 (Page 73, #34)
question:
The diagrams show the difference between the circulatory system of a fish and a mammal. What is the advantage that the circulatory system of the mammal has over the circulatory system of a fish?

&&img&& PAGE_73_Q34 &&img&&
explanation: Double circulation allows oxygenated blood from the lungs to return to the heart and allows the heart to pump the blood under high pressure through the aorta to the rest of the body at high speeds, ensuring efficient transport of blood to the rest of the body. This is unlike the fish, which has a single loop circulatory system that results in oxygenated blood flowing away from the gills to the rest of the body at a much lower pressure.

options.option_text: Blood can be pumped at a higher pressure from the heart to the lungs, allowing more time for gaseous exchange to take place.
Double circulation enables the transport of oxygen in blood to still occur even when the lungs are removed.
Oxygenated blood is pumped at a lower pressure in mammalian circulatory system to the rest of the body, allowing more time for oxygen to diffuse into the cells of different organs.
Oxygenated blood is pumped at a higher pressure in mammalian circulatory system to the rest of the body, allowing more efficient oxygen transport.

title: Question 2 (Page 73, #35)
question:
The diagram shows the changes in the pressure of blood as it flows through various regions of the circulatory system. Identify regions P, Q, R and S.

&&img&& PAGE_73_Q35 &&img&&
explanation: The contraction of the ventricular muscles of the heart will lead to a drastic increase in blood pressure, hence, P is the heart. The blood pressure decreases gradually from the artery (Q) to the capillary (R) and finally the vein (S) before the blood is circulated back to the heart.

options.option_text: P: artery, Q: heart, R: vein, S: capillary
P: capillary, Q: vein, R: artery, S: heart
P: heart, Q: artery, R: capillary, S: vein
P: vein, Q: capillary, R: artery, S: heart

title: Question 3 (Page 73, #36)
question:
Which of these statements explain the fluctuations in blood pressure in region Q?

&&img&& PAGE_73_Q36 &&img&&
explanation: The rhythmic contractions and relaxation of the heart as it pumps causes fluctuations in the arterial blood pressure (Q), leading to a pulse rate. However, as the blood flows further away from the artery, the blood pressure decreases gradually.

options.option_text: Regular contractions of skeletal muscle tissues near the vessel in Q results in fluctuations in blood pressure.
The blood vessels in Q are clogged with fatty tissues, resulting in fluctuations in blood pressure.
The fluctuations in pressure in Q are due to the opening and closing of valves in the blood vessel.
The regular contractions and relaxation of the heart muscles causes the blood pressure in Q to fluctuate.

title: Question 4 (Page 73, #37)
question:
A patient underwent an ABO blood test and discovered that his blood phenotype is that of the AB blood group. Which of the following is the likely result that he obtained from the test?

&&img&& PAGE_73_Q37 &&img&&
explanation: A patient with AB blood group will have both antigen A and antigen B on his red blood cells, hence causing agglutination when added to serum containing antibody-a and antibody-b.

options.option_text: anti-A: no clumping, anti-B: no clumping

title: Question 5 (Page 73, #38)
question:
The diagram shows a transverse section of a human heart. Identify valves 1, 2, 3 and 4.

&&img&& PAGE_73_Q38 &&img&&
explanation: The bicuspid valve is characterised by the presence of two flaps, hence, should be valve 4. The tricuspid valve has three flaps, hence, should be valve 3. The pulmonary and aortic valves are the semi-lunar valves.

options.option_text: valve 1: aortic, valve 2: pulmonary, valve 3: bicuspid, valve 4: tricuspid
valve 1: bicuspid, valve 2: tricuspid, valve 3: pulmonary, valve 4: aortic
valve 1: pulmonary, valve 2: aortic, valve 3: tricuspid, valve 4: bicuspid
valve 1: tricuspid, valve 2: bicuspid, valve 3: aortic, valve 4: pulmonary

title: Question 1 (Page 74, #39)
question:
What will the state of these valves be during ventricular systole?

&&img&& PAGE_74_Q39 &&img&&
explanation: During ventricular systole, the ventricular muscles contract causing the pressure in the ventricles to be higher than the pressure in the atria and the blood vessels. This causes valves 3 and 4 to be closed to prevent backflow of blood from the ventricle to the atrium. The semi-lunar valves (1 and 2) open.

options.option_text: valve 1: closed, valve 2: closed, valve 3: opened, valve 4: opened
valve 1: closed, valve 2: opened, valve 3: closed, valve 4: opened
valve 1: opened, valve 2: closed, valve 3: opened, valve 4: closed
valve 1: opened, valve 2: opened, valve 3: closed, valve 4: closed

title: Question 2 (Page 74, #40)
question: Patients who undergo kidney transplants have to take immunosuppressant drugs to minimise chances of tissue rejection. Which functions of blood is likely to be suppressed using immunosuppressant drugs?
explanation: The component of blood responsible for tissue rejection is the white blood cells comprising lymphocytes and phagocytes. These cells can detect the presence of the foreign kidney cells and attack the kidney by releasing antibodies or carrying out phagocytosis respectively. Hence, immunosuppressant drugs that suppress the antibody production or phagocytosis are needed.

title: Question 3 (Page 74, #41)
question: Soldiers who are expected to remain still for a long period of time during parades are often told to wriggle their toes to maintain blood circulation in the leg. Which of the following best explains why wriggling their toes helps maintain blood circulation?
explanation: Due to the low blood pressure in the veins, muscular contractions around the veins are vital in maintaining smooth blood flow in the veins. The valves in the veins do prevent backflow of blood in the veins. However, this is not affected by the wrapping of toes.

options.option_text: Wriggling toes causes muscular contraction around the veins to help push the blood upwards towards the heart.
Wriggling toes help close the semi-lunar valves in the veins to prevent backflow of blood.
Wriggling toes sends nerve signals to the brain and to the veins, forcing them to contract rhythmically.
Wriggling toes stimulates the adrenal gland to release the hormone adrenaline, which increases heart rate.

title: Question 4 (Page 74, #42)
question:
The graph shows the carbon dioxide concentration of four blood samples taken from different blood vessels, A, B, C and D, in the human body. Which sample of blood is most likely to be taken from the pulmonary artery?

&&img&& PAGE_74_Q42 &&img&&
explanation: The pulmonary artery transports deoxygenated blood from the rest of the body to the lungs, hence it should contain the highest concentration of carbon dioxide.

title: Question 5 (Page 74, #43)
question: What causes the flaps of the atrio-ventricular valves to close during the cardiac cycle?
explanation: When the ventricular muscles contract, the pressure in the ventricles increases and causes the bicuspid and tricuspid valves to close, preventing the backflow of blood from the ventricles into the atria.

options.option_text: contraction of the tendons attached to the valve flaps
increase in pressure of blood as the ventricle contracts
relaxation of the tendons attached to the valve flaps

title: Question 6 (Page 74, #44)
question:
When listening to the hearbeat using a stethoscope, a loud 'lub' sound can be heard, followed very shortly by a softer 'dub' sound. What is the source of the 'lub' sound and the stage of the cardiac cycle when the sound can be heard?

&&img&& PAGE_74_Q44 &&img&&
explanation: During ventricular systole, the increase in blood pressure due to ventricular contraction causes the backflow of blood, which results in the atrio-ventricular valves to slam shut, creating the loud 'lub' sound.

options.option_text: source of sound: closing of atrio-ventricular valves, stage of cardiac cycle: ventricular systole
source of sound: closing of atrio-ventricular valves, stage of cardiac cycle: ventricular diastole
source of sound: closing of semi-lunar valves, stage of cardiac cycle: ventricular systole
source of sound: closing of semi-lunar valves, stage of cardiac cycle: ventricular diastole

title: Question 7 (Page 74, #45)
question: When listening to the hearbeat using a stethoscope, a loud 'lub' sound can be heard, followed very shortly by a softer 'dub' sound. Which of the following explains how the softer 'dub' sound is created?
explanation: The 'dub' sound in the cardiac cycle is caused by the closing of the relatively smaller semi-lunar valves in the aorta and pulmonary artery (compared to the larger atrio-ventricular valves which will produce the louder 'lub' sound).

options.option_text: The blood pressure in the aorta is higher than the blood pressure in the left ventricle, resulting in the backflow of blood that causes the semi-lunar valve to slam shut.
The blood pressure in the aorta is lower than the blood pressure in the left ventricle, resulting in the backflow of blood that causes the semi-lunar valve to slam shut.
The blood pressure in the left ventricle is higher than the blood pressure in the left atrium, resulting in the backflow of blood that causes the tricuspid valve to slam shut.
The blood pressure in the left ventricle is lower than the blood pressure in the left atrium, resulting in the backflow of blood that causes the tricuspid valve to slam shut.

title: Question 1 (Page 75, #46)
question:
Suggest the identities of blood vessels P, Q and T.

&&img&& PAGE_75_Q46 &&img&&
explanation: Vessel P has a high blood pressure, hence, it must be an artery. However, low oxygen levels suggest that it is the pulmonary artery, as it is responsible for transporting deoxygenated blood to the lungs. The blood pressure is low and there is a rapid increase in oxygen levels in vessel Q, suggesting that Q must be the capillaries found in the lungs that is undergoing gaseous exchange. Vessel T brings deoxygenated blood back to the heart, hence must be the vena cava.

options.option_text: vessel P: aorta, vessel Q: capillaries, vessel T: vena cava
vessel P: pulmonary artery, vessel Q: capillaries, vessel T: vena cava
vessel P: pulmonary vein, vessel Q: aorta, vessel T: pulmonary artery
vessel P: vena cava, vessel Q: pulmonary artery, vessel T: aorta

title: Question 2 (Page 75, #47)
question:
Which of these organs is unlikely to be organ S?

&&img&& PAGE_75_Q47 &&img&&
explanation: The urea concentration rises in the blood after passing through organ S, suggesting that S has a high metabolism rate that results in an increase in urea waste production. The kidney will have caused the urea concentration to fall sharply instead as its function is to remove urea from the blood to produce urine, hence, S is unlikely to be the kidney.

title: Question 3 (Page 75, #48)
question:
Suggest the identity of chamber X.

&&img&& PAGE_75_Q48 &&img&&
explanation: The blood pressure is the highest in chamber X. Together with the high oxygen concentration, this suggests that X is the left ventricle that is responsible for pumping blood out of the heart to the rest of the body via aorta.

title: Question 4 (Page 75, #49)
question:
Which substances do 1, 2 and 3 represent respectively?

&&img&& PAGE_75_Q49 &&img&&
explanation: Phagocytes, like all white blood cells, are able to change shape to exit between the capillary walls into the tissue fluid to fight infections. Amino acid is a nutrient that is able to diffuse across the capillary wall into the tissue fluid and into the cells. Urea and carbon dioxide, being waste products will diffuse out of the tissue cells into the tissue fluid and into the capillary. Option B is incorrect as phagocytes do not enter the cells.

title: Question 5 (Page 75, #50)
question:
Which of the following events happen at point P of the cardiac cycle?

1 ventricular wall contracts
2 semi-lunar aortic valves are closed
3 deoxygenated blood flows into left ventricle from left atrium

&&img&& PAGE_75_Q50 &&img&&
explanation: At point P, the ventricular pressure is rising and has just overtaken the atrial pressure, suggesting that the ventricular walls are contracting. Since the ventricular pressure at P is still lower than that of the aorta, the aortic valves are still closed. The blood in the left ventricle and atrium are oxygenated blood from the lungs, hence (3) is incorrect.

title: Question 1 (Page 76, #51)
question:
Which of the following shows the correct explanation for the direction of blood flow?

&&img&& PAGE_76_Q51 &&img&&
explanation: The purpose of the valves is to close when blood is moving in the opposite direction to minimise backflow. The valves shown in the diagram are closed at the moment, opening towards Q as the blood flows from P to Q. Although some veins, such as those found at the legs, do transport blood against flow of gravity, the orientation of the diagram is not specified, hence, it is difficult to determine from which direction gravity is acting upon.

options.option_text: P to Q - The valve flaps open towards direction of Q, hence, blood flow must be from P to Q.
P to Q - The diameter of vein at P is smaller than that of Q, hence, blood flow must be from P to Q.
Q to P - The valve flaps open towards direction of P, hence, blood flow must be from Q to P.
Q to P - Veins transport blood against flow of gravity, hence, blood flow must be from Q to P.

title: Question 2 (Page 76, #52)
question:
Which of the following shows the state of the skeletal muscle and the valves X and Y?

&&img&& PAGE_76_Q52 &&img&&
explanation: When the muscle contracts, the blood pressure increases and forces the blood to move in both directions towards P and Q. This forces valve Y to open as blood flows downwards towards Q. At the same time, valve X will be forced shut as the blood attempts to flow upwards towards P, preventing backflow of blood.

options.option_text: skeletal muscle: contracted, valve X: closed, valve Y: open
skeletal muscle: contracted, valve X: open, valve Y: close
skeletal muscle: relaxed, valve X: closed, valve Y: closed
skeletal muscle: relaxed, valve X: open, valve Y: open

title: Question 3 (Page 76, #53)
question:
Which of the following describes the difference between having a three-chambered heart and a four-chambered heart?

&&img&& PAGE_76_Q53 &&img&&
explanation: Oxygenated blood in the single ventricle of the three-chambered heart will mix with the deoxygenated blood, hence, decreasing the oxygen level in the blood pumped to the rest of the body. Since the deoxygenated blood pumped to the lungs is mixed with oxygenated blood, gaseous exchange in lungs will also be less efficient due to smaller concentration gradient.

title: Question 4 (Page 76, #54)
question:
At which point in the cardiac cycle below does it coincide with the status of the valves as seen in the diagram above?

&&img&& PAGE_76_Q54 &&img&&
explanation: Both the atrio-ventricular valves and semi-lunar valves are shut. To ensure that the atrio-ventricular valves are shut, the pressure of ventricle must be more than that of atrium. To ensure that semi-lunar valves are shut, the pressure of aorta must be more than that of ventricle. Point A fulfils both these prerequisites.

title: Question 1 (Page 77, #55)
question:
The different blood vessels in the body are represented by different letters/short forms as shown below. Which set of graphs correctly represents the data for the different blood vessels in the body?

&&img&& PAGE_77_Q55 &&img&&
explanation: The cross-sectional area of capillaries is the highest due to the high number of capillaries that are found throughout the body. The velocity of blood in arteries are the highest and slows down significantly when blood is moving through the capillaries to enable more time for diffusion of substances. The wall is thicker in the arteries and veins while capillary walls are only one-cell thick. The blood pressure decreases from arteries to capillaries to veins as the blood is transported further from the heart.

options.option_text: Graph set A showing total cross-sectional area, velocity, wall thickness, and pressure patterns for art a c v vn
Graph set B showing total cross-sectional area, velocity, wall thickness, and pressure patterns for art a c v vn
Graph set C showing total cross-sectional area, velocity, wall thickness, and pressure patterns for art a c v vn
Graph set D showing total cross-sectional area, velocity, wall thickness, and pressure patterns for art a c v vn

question:
Name blood vessels X and Y.

explanation: The machine simulates the presence of the lungs. The pulmonary artery brings blood towards the machine and the pulmonary vein brings blood back to the heart from the machine.

vessel X: pulmonary artery, vessel Y: pulmonary vein
vessel X: pulmonary vein, vessel Y: pulmonary artery

title: Question 3 (Page 77, #57)
question:
Which of these chemicals should be added to the blood in the reservoir to keep the heart beating?

1 carbon dioxide
2 glucose
3 anticoagulant
4 oxygen

&&img&& PAGE_77_Q57 &&img&&
explanation: Glucose and oxygen is needed as raw materials to allow the heart muscle to continue respiring and contracting. An anticoagulant, for example, heparin, is needed to minimise chances of coagulation of blood as the blood circulates between the machine and the heart.

title: Question 4 (Page 77, #58)
question:
The diagram shows a type of artery. Identify the type of the artery and vessel X shown.

&&img&& PAGE_77_Q58 &&img&&
explanation: The artery shows presence of valves and only arteries that are connected directly to the heart contain valves. This could either be the aorta or pulmonary artery. Since vessel X is branching off from the artery, it is an arteriole and not a capillary. The capillaries are formed from the branching of arterioles.

options.option_text: identity of artery: aorta, vessel X: arteriole
identity of artery: aorta, vessel X: capillary
identity of artery: hepatic artery, vessel X: arteriole
identity of artery: hepatic artery, vessel X: venule

title: Question 5 (Page 77, #59)
question:
Some features of the human circulatory system are shown below. In which region can platelets be categorised?

&&img&& PAGE_77_Q59 &&img&&
explanation: Platelets are fragments of cells so they do not contain nuclei. During tissue injury, platelets along with the damaged tissues release the enzyme thrombokinase which triggers a series of events that results in the formation of a blood clot, which in turn prevents the entry of foreign bodies and pathogens into the body, hence the platelets' protective function.

title: Question 1 (Page 78, #60)
question:
The electrocardiogram (ECG) shows the electrical activity of the heart of a human at rest. The sharpest increase in the ECG pattern corresponds to ventricular systole of the heart. Using the data between point R and S in the graph above, calculate the average duration of one complete cardiac cycle.

&&img&& PAGE_78_Q60 &&img&&
explanation: Each large square on the scale represents 0.2 s. Point R to point S consists of 19 large squares, hence, the duration will be 0.2 × 19 = 3.8 s. In 3.8 s, there were five more spikes between points R and S, suggesting that there were five complete cycles. Hence, the average duration of one complete cycle will be 3.8 ÷ 5 = 0.76 s.

title: Question 2 (Page 78, #61)
question: High altitude training is often conducted by elite marathon runners to improve their performance before competitions. This involves living and training at locations more than 2000 metres above sea level, where the oxygen concentration is significantly lower. Which of the following statements explains why training in high altitudes may lead to increased performance for a marathon runner?
explanation: Higher altitude training does not lead to more white blood cell production. The body does not have the ability to lose heat quickly if the competition takes place in warmer regions. The difference in gravitational force experienced in high altitudes and at sea level is negligible.

options.option_text: High altitude training leads to production of more white blood cells, which boosts the immunity of the runner, keeping him healthy.
Low oxygen concentrations in higher altitudes will lead to production of more red blood cells, allowing the runner to have increased oxygen carrying ability.
Training at high altitudes where temperatures are lower allows the heat in the body to be dissipated quickly, minimising the chances of heat stroke during training.
The higher gravity experienced in higher altitudes increases the weight at which the runner's legs have to carry, allowing more leg muscles to be built during training.

title: Question 3 (Page 78, #62)
question:
Four samples of blood, W, X, Y and Z, were analysed for their red blood cell, white blood cell and platelet count. Which blood sample was taken from an individual living in a mountainous region?

&&img&& PAGE_78_Q62 &&img&&
explanation: Sample W had the highest red blood cell count among the four samples. A person living in a mountainous region would be exposed to lower oxygen levels. To ensure sufficient oxygen supply in the blood, the body would produce higher than normal levels of red blood cells to compensate for lower levels of atmospheric oxygen.

title: Question 4 (Page 78, #63)
question:
Blood samples X, Y and Z were taken from three patients who are suffering from three different diseases. One of the patients is suffering from thrombocytopaenia, whose wounds take a long time to heal. The other patient suffers from leukaemia that results in increased levels of lymphocytes produced. The last patient suffers from Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome (AIDS) where the body's immunity is greatly weakened due to the destruction of the immune system. Based on the data given, which of the following correctly matches the blood sample of the patients with their corresponding diseases?

&&img&& PAGE_78_Q63 &&img&&
explanation: Thrombocytopaenia is characterised by very low platelet counts in an individual, resulting in difficulty in the clotting of blood and healing of wounds. Since blood sample Y has very low platelet count, it should be the blood sample taken from the patient suffering from thrombocytopaenia. Lymphocytes are a type of white blood cell. Since blood sample X has increased white blood cell count, it should be the blood sample taken from the patient suffering from leukaemia. AIDS patients have a very weak immune system as the white blood cell count is very low, hence, the blood sample taken from an AIDS patient should be Z.

options.option_text: thrombocytopaenia: X, leukaemia: Y, AIDS: Z
thrombocytopaenia: Y, leukaemia: X, AIDS: Z
thrombocytopaenia: Y, leukaemia: Z, AIDS: X
thrombocytopaenia: Z, leukaemia: Y, AIDS: X

title: Question 1 (Page 79, #64)
question: A patient with blood type AB, suffering from dangerously low red blood cell count required emergency transfusion of compatible red blood cells from a donor. The blood from the donor with blood type O was first separated by centrifugation. All components of the donor's blood were removed except the red blood cells before transfusing the blood to the patient. Which of the following is the reason why it is important to remove the blood plasma of the donor before transfusion?
explanation: The donor's blood plasma would contain anti-A and anti-B antibodies, which will cause agglutination when in contact with the donor's red blood cell with A and B antigens.

options.option_text: The blood plasma of the donor contains high levels of urea that will affect the pH level of the patient's blood.
The blood plasma of the donor contains water that may increase the water potential of the patient's blood, leading to lysis of red blood cells.
The blood plasma of the donor may contain antibodies that may attack the antigens found on the patient's red blood cells and cause agglutination.
The blood plasma of the donor may contain pathogens that will make the patient sick.

title: Question 2 (Page 79, #65)
question:
Jane was born with congenital ventricular septal defect, with the presence of a hole at the inner wall between the two ventricles. As a result of this defect, Jane often found herself feeling breathless easily and could not participate in strenuous physical activities. The diagram shows a heart with ventricular septal defect. Which of the following explains Jane's symptoms whenever she exerts herself?

&&img&& PAGE_79_Q65 &&img&&
explanation: Due to the relatively higher blood pressure in the left ventricle compared to the right, blood tends to flow from the left to the right ventricle through the gap. This results in the mixing of the blood and less oxygenated blood will then be pumped to the rest of the body.

options.option_text: The gap between the ventricles causes less blood to be transported to the lungs, causing less oxygen to be transported to the rest of the body.
The gap between the ventricles leads to the mixing of deoxygenated and oxygenated blood, causing less oxygen to be transported to the rest of the body.
The gap between the ventricles results in a decreased ventricular pressure, causing the backflow of blood into the atria as the atrio-ventricular valves remain open during ventricular contraction.
The gap between the ventricles results in thinner ventricular muscle walls, hence blood is pumped at slower speeds to the rest of the body, hence decreasing the rate of oxygen intake by the body.

title: Question 3 (Page 79, #66)
question: A baby was born with a genetic condition that results in the weakening of the walls of the aorta, giving rise to a thinner muscle and elastic tissue layer than the normal aorta. Which will not be a likely consequence of such a genetic condition?
explanation: Thinner aortic walls will lead to the aorta being less able to withstand the high pressure of the blood pumped out during ventricular systole. This may lead to rupturing of the aorta. The lack of elastic tissues will also lead to blood pressure decreasing at a faster rate as the blood moves away from the heart. With a thinner muscle and elastic tissue layer, the lumen will widen and should not restrict blood flow through the aorta.

options.option_text: restriction of blood flow through the aorta
rupturing of aorta due to high blood pressure
widening of the lumen of the aorta

title: Question 4 (Page 79, #67)
question:
The table shows the results of a blood group testing done for three patients, Anna, Bella and Cherise. Blood serum isolated from blood group AB and blood group O was added into each of the blood samples from the three patients. Based on results from testing their blood with serum from blood group O, which of the three patients had type O blood?

&&img&& PAGE_79_Q67 &&img&&
explanation: Serum from blood group O contains antibodies against both antigen A and antigen B. Since Bella's blood did not agglutinate when the serum was added, Bella's blood do not contain antigen A or B. This means Bella's blood was of type O.

options.option_text: None of them had type O blood

title: Question 5 (Page 79, #68)
question:
Which of the following conclusions could be made based on the result of the blood test conducted above?

&&img&& PAGE_79_Q68 &&img&&
explanation: Anna's blood, just like Cherise's, agglutinated when exposed to serum from blood group O, suggesting that her blood had either antigen A or B or had both antigen A and B, hence her possible blood groups were A, B or AB. Since red blood cells from blood type O has no A or B antigens, there would not be any agglutination, hence Anna's blood could not be of type O. Bella, having blood type O, was a universal donor, hence, would be able to donate blood to both Anna and Cherise. Since the possible blood groups for Cherise and Anna were A, B or AB, Cherise might not be able to donate her blood to Anna if Anna's blood type was not AB.

options.option_text: Anna had a blood type of A, B or AB but not O.
Anna had a blood type of either A or not AB.
Cherise and Anna definitely had the same blood type.
Cherise had a blood type of AB but not A or B.

title: Question 1 (Page 80, #69)
question:
There is often a frequent shortage of certain blood types during large scale emergencies. Scientists have discovered that an enzyme, α1,3-galactosidase, extracted from a bacteria found in the human gut, Bacteroides fragilis, is able to remove the B antigens from the red blood cell of donated blood type B as shown in the diagram below. What will the implications of removing antigens B from the red blood cell of type B blood be?

&&img&& PAGE_80_Q69 &&img&&
explanation: Removing antigens B from the red blood cells of blood type B results in the production of red blood cells without antigens, hence, transforming it into type O blood. Since type O blood has no antigens, it can be donated to any ABO blood group recipient. However, this enzyme does not remove any antibodies that are present in the serum of the blood.

options.option_text: allows blood to be donated to all ABO blood groups
converts type B blood into type A blood
makes blood more resistant to infections
removes antibody b from the serum of the donated blood

title: Question 2 (Page 80, #70)
question:
Between which of the four points, A, B, C or D, will the bicuspid valve remain closed?

&&img&& PAGE_80_Q70 &&img&&
explanation: The bicuspid valve remains closed when ventricular pressure is higher than atrial pressure between A and D.

title: Question 3 (Page 80, #71)
question:
Which points in the diagram coincide with the 'lub' and 'dub' sounds of the heart respectively?

&&img&& PAGE_80_Q71 &&img&&
explanation: At point A, the ventricular pressure is higher than the atrial pressure, causing the bicuspid valve to slam shut and produce a 'lub' sound. At point C, the aortic pressure is higher than the ventricular pressure, causing the semi-lunar aortic valve to slam shut and produce a 'dub' sound.

title: Question 4 (Page 80, #72)
question:
From the diagram given, estimate the heart rate (beats per minute) of this individual.

&&img&& PAGE_80_Q72 &&img&&
explanation: From the graph, the sharp increase in ventricular pressure, suggesting that it is the start of ventricular systole, begins just before 0.2 s and again at 0.8 s. This means that one complete heartbeat takes (0.8 - 0.2) = 0.6 s. To measure the heart rate per minute, divide the number of seconds in a minute with the time per heartbeat: 60 ÷ 0.6 =100 beats per minute

title: Question 5 (Page 80, #73)
question:
What is the ratio of the timing of atrial systole to atrial diastole?

&&img&& PAGE_80_Q73 &&img&&
explanation: From the diagram, atrial systole occurs between 0.0 s to 0.2 s. Since the complete cardiac cycle in the diagram is 0.6 s long, duration of atrial diastole should be 0.6 - 0.2 = 0.4 s.

title: Question 6 (Page 80, #74)
question:
A patient underwent a surgical procedure known as angioplasty, whereby a catheter with an expandable stent is inserted into the blocked coronary artery. The diagram below shows the details of the surgical procedure. Which of the following events will happen after the successful completion of the surgery?

1 decrease in cholesterol levels in blood
2 increase in oxygenated blood supply to the heart muscles
3 decrease in blood pressure

&&img&& PAGE_80_Q74 &&img&&
explanation: The surgical procedure increases the diameter of the lumen of the coronary artery, leading to an increase in the blood supply to the heart muscle and a decrease in blood pressure. However, cholesterol levels in the blood is unaffected by the medical procedure and must be controlled with medicine and changes in diet.

title: Question 1 (Page 81, #75)
question:
A blood sample from three blood vessels in a healthy individual is analysed for concentrations of oxygen and glucose. The results are recorded in the table below. Jason is suffering from a disease and blood samples from similar blood vessels are taken from him and analysed for concentrations of oxygen and glucose. The results are recorded in the table below. Based on the information given above, what disease is Jason likely to be suffering from?

&&img&& PAGE_81_Q75 &&img&&
explanation: The oxygen and glucose concentration in Jason's coronary artery is lower than average, however, the oxygen and glucose concentration in the other blood vessels are of average value. This shows that there is a lower volume of blood being provided to the coronary artery, which might suggest that the coronary artery is blocked and its lumen narrowed. This is a symptom of atherosclerosis.

title: Question 2 (Page 81, #76)
question:
The diagram shows an arteriovenous fistula created in the arm of a dialysis patient. An arteriovenous fistula is a passageway between an artery and a vein which can be surgically created for the dialysis patients. Which of the following will be the result of creating an arteriovenous fistula in the arm?

&&img&& PAGE_81_Q76 &&img&&
explanation: As blood from the artery is sent directly to the vein through the arteriovenous fistula, the blood pressure in the vein will increase. This eventually causes the muscle layer in the vein to thicken to withstand the higher blood pressure. The artery will never develop valves regardless of the change in blood pressure.

options.option_text: The artery starts to develop valves to prevent backflow of blood.
The blood oxygen content in the vein will decrease.
The urea content in the vein will increase.
The vein starts to develop thicker muscle layer.

title: Question 1 (Page 82, #1)
question: Which row shows the correct word equation for aerobic respiration?
explanation: During aerobic respiration, glucose is oxidised completely in the presence of oxygen to carbon dioxide and water, with a large amount of energy liberated in the process.

glucose + oxygen → lactic acid + water + energy

question: Which row shows the correct word equation for anaerobic respiration in muscles?
explanation: During anaerobic respiration in muscles, glucose is broken down in the absence of oxygen to produce only lactic acid. A small amount of energy is liberated in this process.

glucose → lactic acid + carbon dioxide + water + energy

title: Question 3 (Page 82, #3)
question: Which of the following processes does not result in an overall loss of energy?
explanation: Cellular respiration releases energy. The rest of the processes in options B, C and D require energy and use up energy that is provided by respiration.

question:

1 It occurs in all living cells.
2 It occurs all the time.
3 Oxygen, carbon dioxide and water are produced.
4 Energy is released.
5 Food is oxidised.
explanation: During aerobic respiration, carbon dioxide and water are produced, but oxygen is not produced. Thus statement 3 is incorrect. The products of anaerobic respiration are different. The other descriptions would apply to both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

title: Question 5 (Page 82, #5)

explanation: The build-up of lactic acid in the muscles causes fatigue.

options.option_text: increase surface area for gaseous exchange
produce mucus to trap dust particles

question: Which of the following components in cigarette smoke increases the risk of lung cancer?

title: Question 8 (Page 82, #8)
question: Which of the following components in cigarette smoke increases the risk of atherosclerosis?

title: Question 9 (Page 82, #9)
question: Why is carbon monoxide in cigarette smoke harmful?
explanation: Carbon monoxide binds irreversibly with haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin, and this decreases the amount of effective haemoglobin that can transport oxygen in the red blood cells.

options.option_text: It paralyses the cilia lining the trachea.

question: Which of the following statements about respiration is true?
explanation: During oxidation of glucose, chemical potential energy is converted into heat, kinetic, sound and other forms of energy. Intestinal villi make use of energy released from aerobic respiration for active transport of glucose.

options.option_text: During oxidation of glucose, chemical potential energy is converted into other forms of energy.
Energy is used up during vigorous exercise so anaerobic respiration occurs.
A lot of energy is released during anaerobic respiration to supplement the body's requirements during exercise.
Intestinal villi make use of energy released from anaerobic respiration to absorb glucose by active transport when oxygen levels are low.

title: Question 1 (Page 83, #11)
question:

&&img&& PAGE_83_Q11 &&img&&
explanation: When the race concludes, the lactic acid concentration in the muscles will start to decrease as the lactic acid is slowly oxidised.

title: Question 2 (Page 83, #12)
question: Which of the following processes does not result in a net loss of energy in humans?
explanation: Breathing, peristalsis and sleeping, all involve the use of muscles and therefore energy will be expended. Respiration releases energy from glucose and does not result in a net loss of energy.

title: Question 3 (Page 83, #13)
question:
Which arrow shows the movement of oxygen during inspiration?

&&img&& PAGE_83_Q13 &&img&&
explanation: During inspiration, there is a higher concentration of oxygen in the alveolus, so oxygen diffuses from the alveolus into the blood capillaries. Oxygen is carried by the red blood cells, not the plasma, so arrow C is the correct answer.

Based only on this diagram, which statement is not true?

One-cell-thick endothelial wall enables efficient diffusion of dissolved gases.

cell X: epithelial cell, cell Y: ciliated cell

title: Question 3 (Page 85, #29)
question:
Which adaptations of the alveoli decreases the diffusion distance of gases?
