title: Question 4 (Page 85, #30)
question: In the lungs, oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged at the alveoli surfaces. By which process does this gaseous exchange occur?
explanation: In the lungs, oxygen gas dissolves into the thin film of moisture lining the alveolar walls, then diffuse across into the surrounding blood capillaries to bind with haemoglobin in the red blood cells. Carbon dioxide from the blood plasma, diffuses from the blood capillaries into the alveoli and is removed when a person exhales.

title: Question 5 (Page 85, #31)
question: Which of the following comparisons between respiration and breathing in humans is incorrect?
explanation: Respiration is a process that releases energy. Breathing, on the other hand, requires energy, as the muscles involved (e.g. diaphragm, intercostal muscles) need to alternately contract and relax.

options.option_text: respiration: chemical reaction, breathing: not a chemical reaction
respiration: does not involve muscles, breathing: involves muscles
respiration: occurs in all cells, breathing: occurs only in the respiratory tract
respiration: overall expends energy, breathing: overall releases energy

title: Question 6 (Page 85, #32)
question:
Which properties enable the alveoli to increase gas exchange efficiency?

1 constant flow of blood surrounding alveoli
2 equal concentrations of oxygen inside and outside of alveoli
3 one-cell-thick walls
explanation: The constant flow of blood surrounding the alveoli helps to maintain a steep concentration gradient of gases, increasing the rate of diffusion. The one-cell-thick walls of the alveoli also decreases the diffusion distance of gases, also increasing the rate of diffusion.

title: Question 7 (Page 85, #33)
question: Which of the following is a consequence of smoking tobacco?
explanation: Carbon monoxide present in tobacco smoke reduces the oxygen transport efficiency of red blood cells by binding irreversibly to the haemoglobin.

options.option_text: reduced oxygen transport by red blood cells

title: Question 8 (Page 85, #34)
question:
The table shows the percentage composition of three gases in inspired and expired air. Identify gases P, Q and R.

&&img&& PAGE_85_Q34 &&img&&
explanation: Inspired air contains about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide.

options.option_text: gas P: carbon dioxide, gas Q: nitrogen, gas R: oxygen
gas P: nitrogen, gas Q: oxygen, gas R: water vapour
gas P: oxygen, gas Q: nitrogen, gas R: carbon dioxide
gas P: water vapour, gas Q: carbon dioxide, gas R: oxygen

title: Question 1 (Page 86, #35)
question:
The following table shows the percentage composition of four samples of air. Which sample could have been breathed out by a person with emphysema?

&&img&& PAGE_86_Q35 &&img&&
explanation: A person with emphysema has reduced alveolar surface area for gaseous exchange, hence, efficiency of diffusion of gases is lower compared to a healthy individual. A healthy individual breathes out air that has approximately 16% oxygen, 4% carbon dioxide and saturated with water vapour. A person with emphysema hence breathes out air that will have a higher oxygen and lower carbon dioxide percentage comparatively.

options.option_text: 14% oxygen, 0.5% carbon dioxide, saturated water vapour
16% oxygen, 4% carbon dioxide, unsaturated water vapour
18% oxygen, 3% carbon dioxide, saturated water vapour
21% oxygen, 0.04% carbon dioxide, unsaturated water vapour

title: Question 2 (Page 86, #36)
question:
The diagram represents the relationship between tissue cells and capillaries in the movement of carbon dioxide. Which point, A, B, C or D, is most affected by pH fluctuations?

&&img&& PAGE_86_Q36 &&img&&
explanation: The formation of carbonic acid, H2CO3, from carbon dioxide, CO2, and water, H2O, is catalysed by carbonic anhydrase. Since carbonic anhydrase is an enzyme, the reaction will be most affected by pH and temperature changes.

title: Question 3 (Page 86, #37)
question: Which of the following does not produce carbon dioxide?
explanation: Blood and cardiac muscles contain cells that respire to produce carbon dioxide. Mitochondria too will produce carbon dioxide as it is the site of aerobic respiration. Saliva does not contain any living cells, so it will not produce any carbon dioxide.

title: Question 4 (Page 86, #38)
question:
During periods of vigorous exercise, some biochemical changes take place in the muscle tissues. Which row shows the changes that take place compared to resting conditions in the muscles?

&&img&& PAGE_86_Q38 &&img&&
explanation: During extended periods of vigorous exercise, the muscle cells will respire anaerobically to meet the energy demands of the body. Glycogen will be converted into glucose, which is the substrate for respiration. Lactic acid produced during anaerobic respiration will cause the pH to be decreased.

title: Question 5 (Page 86, #39)
question:
Which of the following gases show a higher percentage composition in expired air than inspired air?

1 carbon dioxide 
2 nitrogen
3 oxygen 
4 water vapour
explanation: In exhaled air, the percentage composition of carbon dioxide and water vapour increases as shown in the table, while that of oxygen decreases. This is due to respiration where oxygen is used up, while carbon dioxide and water are produced as waste products and removed during exhalation.

title: Question 6 (Page 86, #40)
question: Which of the following increases first when a person takes part in a sprinting race?
explanation: The muscles first respire aerobically during a race to produce carbon dioxide. This causes the blood plasma carbon dioxide concentration to increase and hence, increases the breathing rate. The increased breathing rate also means that oxygen is taken in faster and more oxygen will be available to the muscles.

title: Question 7 (Page 86, #41)
question:
What is the appearance of the limewater in flasks 2 and 4 after ten minutes?

&&img&& PAGE_86_Q41 &&img&&
explanation: Air that enters flask 2 has no carbon dioxide as potassium hydroxide solution has absorbed all the atmospheric carbon dioxide gas. As a result, the air that is bubbled through the limewater in flask 2 will cause the limewater to remain clear. Air that enters flask 4 contains a high carbon dioxide concentration due to the exhaled carbon dioxide from the respiring snails. The carbon dioxide gas reacts with limewater to produce significant amounts of white precipitate that gives the limewater a cloudy appearance.

title: Question 8 (Page 86, #42)
question:
Which comparison about the air entering and leaving flask 3 is correct?

&&img&& PAGE_86_Q42 &&img&&
explanation: Air that enters flask 3 has a higher oxygen percentage compared to that leaving flask 3, as the snails have taken in some oxygen during respiration.

options.option_text: entering flask 3: higher nitrogen percentage, leaving flask 3: lower nitrogen percentage
entering flask 3: higher oxygen percentage, leaving flask 3: lower oxygen percentage
entering flask 3: higher water vapour percentage, leaving flask 3: lower water vapour percentage
entering flask 3: warmer, leaving flask 3: cooler

title: Question 1 (Page 87, #43)
question: Which of the following conclusions based on this experiment is correct?
explanation: During aerobic respiration, the snails release carbon dioxide which reacts with the limewater in flask 4 to produce a cloudy appearance.

options.option_text: The limewater in flask 2 absorbs oxygen.
The snails respire aerobically to release carbon dioxide.
Unused oxygen that enters flask 4 reacts with the limewater.
The snails will die if the experiment extends too long as the oxygen supply gets depleted.

title: Question 2 (Page 87, #44)
question:
A student sets up an experiment to study anaerobic respiration by yeast cells in sugar solution as shown below. The hydrogencarbonate indicator solution changes colour depending on the pH of the indicator solution. As pH increases from 7 all through to pH 9, the indicator changes from yellow to red to purple. If the test tube containing yeast cells in sugar solution is immersed in a 35°C water bath for two hours, what will be the expected colour of the hydrogencarbonate indicator?

&&img&& PAGE_87_Q44 &&img&&
explanation: Yeast cells undergo anaerobic respiration to produce carbon dioxide which will lead to a decrease in pH of the solution. Hydrogencarbonate indicator turns yellow when pH levels are low.

title: Question 3 (Page 87, #45)
question: What causes the muscle cells to develop an oxygen debt?
explanation: The muscle cells respire anaerobically so that there is energy for the muscles to contract even though there is insufficient oxygen to 'pay' for the energy. In this case, an oxygen debt is incurred and when oxygen is next available, it will be used to 'pay back the debt'.

options.option_text: increased carbon dioxide concentration in blood plasma

title: Question 4 (Page 87, #46)
question:
Which row shows the changes that occur when a person is taking part in vigorous exercise?

&&img&& PAGE_87_Q46 &&img&&
explanation: During vigorous exercise, breathing rate increases and lung tidal volume increases so that the carbon dioxide produced by the muscles can be removed and more oxygen can be taken in for the respiring muscles.

options.option_text: breathing rate decreases, lung tidal volume increases
breathing rate decreases, lung tidal volume remains constant
breathing rate increases, lung tidal volume increases
breathing rate increases, lung tidal volume remains constant

title: Question 5 (Page 87, #47)
question:
The graph shows the volume changes in a person's lungs during breathing when he is at rest. Which graph shows the volume changes in his lungs during vigorous exercise?

&&img&& PAGE_87_Q47 &&img&&
explanation: During vigorous exercise, a person takes more breaths and deeper breaths in order to expel the carbon dioxide produced by the muscles and to take in more oxygen for aerobic respiration.

options.option_text: volume of air in lungs during breathing/dm³ graph showing higher amplitude and same frequency
volume of air in lungs during breathing/dm³ graph showing same amplitude and higher frequency
volume of air in lungs during breathing/dm³ graph showing much higher amplitude and higher frequency
volume of air in lungs during breathing/dm³ graph showing same amplitude and same frequency

title: Question 6 (Page 87, #48)
question:
The diagram shows part of the human respiratory system. Which structures contain muscles that contract during inhalation?

&&img&& PAGE_87_Q48 &&img&&
explanation: During inhalation, the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract. These structures are represented by Z and Y respectively.

title: Question 1 (Page 88, #49)
question:
Which comparison of inhaled and exhaled air is correct?

&&img&& PAGE_88_Q49 &&img&&
explanation: Exhaled air is warmer and has less oxygen, more carbon dioxide and more water vapour.

options.option_text: inhaled air: cooler, exhaled air: warmer
inhaled air: less oxygen, exhaled air: more oxygen
inhaled air: more carbon dioxide, exhaled air: less carbon dioxide
inhaled air: more water vapour, exhaled air: less water vapour

title: Question 2 (Page 88, #50)
question:
What is the volume of air taken in by the athlete after exercise during the 12 seconds?

&&img&& PAGE_88_Q50 &&img&&
explanation: The athlete takes eight breaths, each with a volume of 1 dm³. So the total volume of air breathed in by the athlete is 8 × 1 dm³ = 8 dm³.

title: Question 3 (Page 88, #51)
question:
Which of the following analysis of the results is true?

&&img&& PAGE_88_Q51 &&img&&
explanation: The athlete takes three breaths in 12 seconds when he is at rest. By proportion, he will take a total of 5 × 3 breaths in 60 seconds. His lung capacity remains the same before and after exercise; only the volume of air breathed in increases after exercise.

options.option_text: The athlete's breathing rate doubled after exercise.
The athlete takes about 15 breaths per minute at rest.
The athlete's lung capacity increases after exercise.
The athlete's lung volume decreases after exercise.

title: Question 4 (Page 88, #52)
question:
In the experimental set-up, a person breathes in and out ten times through tube X. What is the appearance of the limewater in test tubes 1 and 2 after ten breaths?

&&img&& PAGE_88_Q52 &&img&&
explanation: When the person breathes in, air is taken in through tube 2. Since there is a low concentration of carbon dioxide in atmospheric air, the limewater in tube 2 remains clear. When the person breathes out, air is removed through tube 1. Since expired air contains a higher concentration of carbon dioxide, a white precipitate will be produced in the limewater in tube 1, giving it a milky appearance.

options.option_text: test tube 1: clear, test tube 2: clear
test tube 1: clear, test tube 2: milky
test tube 1: milky, test tube 2: clear
test tube 1: milky, test tube 2: milky

title: Question 5 (Page 88, #53)
question:
The diagram shows an experimental set-up used to investigate respiration in germinating seeds. In which direction will the indicator fluid move? Why?

&&img&& PAGE_88_Q53 &&img&&
explanation: During respiration, oxygen is taken in and carbon dioxide is given out. However, the soda lime absorbs the carbon dioxide produced. This causes the volume of air in the test tube to decrease. Air in the capillary tube moves into the test tube to replace the oxygen taken in by the germinating seeds, hence, the indicator fluid moves towards the test tube.

options.option_text: direction: away from test tube, explanation: carbon dioxide produced
direction: away from test tube, explanation: oxygen produced
direction: towards test tube, explanation: carbon dioxide taken in
direction: towards test tube, explanation: oxygen taken in

title: Question 1 (Page 89, #54)
question:
The graph shows the changes in air pressure that occur in the lungs during one breathing cycle. At which point of the graph are the ribs moving upwards and outwards?

&&img&& PAGE_89_Q54 &&img&&
explanation: The ribs move upwards and outwards when a person is starting to inhale, which is characterised by a decrease in lung pressure.

title: Question 2 (Page 89, #55)
question:
An apparatus was set up to detect the components of cigarette smoke. A cigarette was smoked by drawing air through the apparatus for fifteen minutes. A new cigarette was added to replace the previous whenever the cigarette had finished burning. Suggest the materials detected in the following parts of the apparatus.

&&img&& PAGE_89_Q55 &&img&&
explanation: Tar found in cigarette smoke tend to be trapped by the cotton wool and stained the cotton wool brown. Carbon dioxide, which will form a white precipitate when it reacts with limewater, will be emitted in this experiment due to combustion of carbon compounds found in the cigarette.

options.option_text: cotton wool: nicotine, limewater: carbon monoxide
cotton wool: nicotine, limewater: carbon dioxide
cotton wool: tar, limewater: carbon monoxide
cotton wool: tar, limewater: carbon dioxide

title: Question 3 (Page 89, #56)
question:
Some chemical reactions and their associated enthalpy changes are shown below. Which of the following statements is true?

&&img&& PAGE_89_Q56 &&img&&
explanation: Alcoholic fermentation by yeast cells and the partial oxidation of glucose by muscle cells break down glucose in the absence of oxygen to release relatively small amounts of energy compared to complete oxidation of glucose in the presence of oxygen. Statement A is not true as anaerobic respiration in muscle cells does not produce carbon dioxide. Statement B is not true as in the presence of oxygen, a lot more energy is released in the breakdown of glucose. Statement D is not true as alcoholic fermentation by yeast cells produces ethanol, while partial oxidation of glucose by muscle cells produces lactic acid.

options.option_text: All types of respiration produce carbon dioxide.
In the presence of oxygen, a lot of energy is absorbed to break down glucose.
Only a small amount of energy is released during anaerobic respiration.
The products of anaerobic respiration in muscle cells and yeast cells are the same.

title: Question 4 (Page 89, #57)
question:
The breathing rates of four different people doing three different activities, one immediately after the other, are shown in the following table. Which person was likely to be leisurely strolling, swimming then sitting down reading a book?

&&img&& PAGE_89_Q57 &&img&&
explanation: The sitting act takes the least amount of energy, so the breathing rate will be the lowest, followed by that of leisurely strolling and then swimming.

title: Question 1 (Page 90, #58)
question:
Historically, many polio patients whose chest muscles were damaged by the polio virus, spent plenty of their time in pressurised chambers known as 'iron lungs'. The patient would be placed in a fully enclosed chamber with only his head sticking out, and alternating changes in the pressure within the chamber mimicked the air pressure within his thorax to help the patient breathe as shown in the diagram below. Which row correctly shows the manipulation of the positive and negative pressure valves to mimic the inhalation stage of breathing?

&&img&& PAGE_90_Q58 &&img&&
explanation: During inhalation, the pressure in the thoracic cavity should be lower than that of atmospheric pressure. In this way, air will rush to fill in the lungs. To achieve low pressure in the thoracic cavity, the negative pressure valve should turn on while the positive pressure valve should turn off.

options.option_text: positive pressure valve: off, negative pressure valve: off
positive pressure valve: off, negative pressure valve: on
positive pressure valve: on, negative pressure valve: off
positive pressure valve: on, negative pressure valve: on

title: Question 2 (Page 90, #59)
question:
Goblet cells lining the trachea, produce mucus which helps to trap dust and other particles. Which organelles listed will be found in high abundance in goblet cells?

1 centriole
2 mitochondria
3 ribosomes
4 vacuoles
explanation: Mucus is made up primarily of proteins which are produced by membrane bound ribosomes. Since protein synthesis is a very energy-consuming process, mitochondria will be present in high abundance to provide energy to the goblet cell.

title: Question 3 (Page 90, #60)
question: How many cell membranes does a molecule of oxygen have to pass through, in order to get from the surrounding air until it combines with haemoglobin in the blood?
explanation: The oxygen molecule has to pass through the alveolar wall, the endothelial wall of the capillary and the plasma membrane of the red blood cell before it is able to reach the haemoglobin.

title: Question 4 (Page 90, #61)
question: When a person is coughing, which of the following changes occur in his chest?
explanation: Coughing is akin to breathing out with a greater force. This thus causes the internal intercostal muscles to contract more strongly, as a result, causes the rib cage to drop down even further.

options.option_text: internal intercostal muscles: contract, rib cage: moves downwards
internal intercostal muscles: contract, rib cage: moves upwards
internal intercostal muscles: relax, rib cage: moves downwards
internal intercostal muscles: relax, rib cage: moves upwards

title: Question 5 (Page 90, #62)
question:
The graph shows changes in the air pressure that takes place within the lungs during one breathing cycle. What causes the change in air pressure during stage 1?

&&img&& PAGE_90_Q62 &&img&&
explanation: When the diaphragm muscles contract, the volume in the lungs increases, causing a decrease in air pressure in the lungs. The low air pressure causes surrounding air to flow into the lungs (inhalation). The increase in volume of air in the lungs causes the air pressure to slowly increase (stages 2 and 3).

options.option_text: movement of air into the lungs
movement of air out of the lungs

title: Question 6 (Page 90, #63)
question:
At which stage in the breathing cycle is there outflow of air from the lungs?

&&img&& PAGE_90_Q63 &&img&&
explanation: When air pressure in the lungs is higher than that of the surrounding air, air in the lungs will flow out of the lungs into the surrounding air (exhalation).

title: Question 1 (Page 91, #64)
question: Which of the following does not explain why a person's heart rate increases during exercise?
explanation: Lactic acid is brought from the muscles to the liver for oxidation.

options.option_text: to bring carbon dioxide to the lungs for removal
to bring glucose to the muscles for energy release
to bring lactic acid to the muscles for oxidation
to bring oxygen to the muscles for respiration

title: Question 2 (Page 91, #65)
question:
Which group of bars could represent the large intestine?

&&img&& PAGE_91_Q65 &&img&&
explanation: In times of exercise, more blood is delivered to the muscles, lungs and liver and less blood is delivered to other organs in the body so that there is sufficient glucose and oxygen for the working muscles.

title: Question 3 (Page 91, #66)
question:
Which organs can be represented by the cluster of bars in A?

1 heart
2 lungs
3 muscles
4 pancreas
5 spleen

&&img&& PAGE_91_Q66 &&img&&
explanation: During exercise, more blood is sent to the heart as the heart is beating more frequently to deliver oxygen and glucose to the contracting muscles. Blood flow also increases in the lungs to collect oxygen and remove carbon dioxide. As the muscles are working harder during or after exercise, blood flow is increased to remove carbon dioxide and to provide oxygen and glucose for respiration.

title: Question 1 (Page 92, #1)
question:
In which labelled part(s) does ultrafiltration occur?

&&img&& PAGE_92_Q1 &&img&&
explanation: Ultrafiltration occurs in the Bowman's capsule (1).

title: Question 2 (Page 92, #2)
question:
In which labelled part(s) does selective reabsorption occur?

&&img&& PAGE_92_Q2 &&img&&
explanation: Selective reabsorption occurs throughout most parts of the kidney nephron, starting from the proximal convoluted tubule, all the way through to the collecting duct.

title: Question 3 (Page 92, #3)
question:
In which regions does anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) affect the permeability of membranes to water?

&&img&& PAGE_92_Q3 &&img&&
explanation: ADH increases the permeability of primarily the collecting ducts and to a small extent, the distal convoluted tubule, to water. This causes the kidney tubules to reabsorb more water, producing less urine that has a higher concentration of metabolic waste solutes.

title: Question 4 (Page 92, #4)
question:
In a healthy individual, which of the labelled parts would contain the highest concentration of glucose?

&&img&& PAGE_92_Q4 &&img&&
explanation: Most glucose would be found in the Bowman's capsule right after ultrafiltration and in the proximal convoluted tubule before selective reabsorption occurs.

title: Question 5 (Page 92, #5)
question:
Which blood vessel contains the highest concentration of urea?

&&img&& PAGE_92_Q5 &&img&&
explanation: Blood that enters the kidney via the renal artery will have the highest concentration of urea while blood that leaves the kidney via the renal vein will have the lowest concentration of urea.

title: Question 6 (Page 92, #6)
question:
Identify structures X, Y and Z in the diagram.

&&img&& PAGE_92_Q6 &&img&&
explanation: The blood in vessel X is transported towards the heart, suggesting that X is the renal vein. Vessel Y receives blood from the heart, thus, will be the renal artery. Tube Z is not a blood vessel but the ureter that contains urine and leaves the kidney directly to the bladder.

options.option_text: X: hepatic vein, Y: hepatic artery, Z: urethra
X: hepatic vein, Y: hepatic artery, Z: ureter
X: renal vein, Y: renal artery, Z: urethra
X: renal vein, Y: renal artery, Z: ureter

title: Question 7 (Page 92, #7)
question:
Which structure has the highest and lowest urea concentration?

&&img&& PAGE_92_Q7 &&img&&
explanation: The ureter has the highest concentration of urea as all the urea from the body is filtered into the kidney nephrons and concentrated in urine which is transported from the kidney to the bladder via the ureter. Blood that flows away from the kidney via the renal vein will then have the lowest concentration of urea.

title: Question 1 (Page 93, #8)
question: What is the function of the bladder?
explanation: The bladder stores urine temporarily until it is discharged from the person's body.

title: Question 2 (Page 93, #9)
question: Which of the following is not an example of excretion?
explanation: Excretion is the removal of metabolic waste products. Undigested food is not an example of metabolic waste as it is not used by the body at all.

options.option_text: removal of carbon dioxide during exhalation

title: Question 3 (Page 93, #10)
question: The kidneys function to remove metabolic waste and maintain a constant blood composition. Which term can be used to describe this function?
explanation: The kidneys remove metabolic waste in a process known as excretion in order to maintain a blood composition that has a low concentration of waste products. This maintenance of a constant internal environment is known as homeostasis.

title: Question 4 (Page 93, #11)
question:
The diagram shows a kidney and some associated blood vessels. Which row shows the correct relative concentrations of urea in the different vessels, X, Y and Z?

&&img&& PAGE_93_Q11 &&img&&
explanation: Vessels carrying blood towards the kidney would have a high concentration of urea (but not the highest) while vessels carrying blood away from the kidney would have a low concentration of urea. The ureter contains a concentrated solution of urea as a composition of urine and hence, the urine would have the highest concentration of urea.

title: Question 5 (Page 93, #12)
question:
Which of the labelled structures are involved in the formation of urine?

&&img&& PAGE_93_Q12 &&img&&
explanation: The liver (P) deaminates excess amino acids to form urea. This urea is transported by blood to the kidney (Q) which then passes out of the collecting duct into the renal pelvis as urine. The bladder (S) stores urine but has no role in the formation of urine.

title: Question 6 (Page 93, #13)
question:
Identify structures P, Q, R and S.

&&img&& PAGE_93_Q13 &&img&&
explanation: Students should be familiar with the naming of the various organs in the body, including those associated with the urinary system.

options.option_text: P: liver, Q: kidney, R: pancreas, S: bladder
P: liver, Q: ureter, R: spleen, S: kidney
P: stomach, Q: kidney, R: pancreas, S: bladder
P: stomach, Q: ureter, R: spleen, S: kidney

title: Question 7 (Page 93, #14)
question:
Some human organs are listed below. 
1 kidneys, 2 pancreas, 3 lungs, 4 skin. 
Which organ(s) excrete(s) nitrogenous compounds?
explanation: The skin removes nitrogenous waste products in the form of sweat, although this is present in sweat in very minute amounts. The kidney is the main excretory organ of nitrogenous waste in the form of urine.

title: Question 8 (Page 93, #15)
question: Which row correctly identifies the vessel that transports urea to the kidneys and the structure that transports urine away from the kidneys towards the bladder?
explanation: Students should be well acquainted with the various structures surrounding the kidney and their associated functions.

options.option_text: urea to the kidney: hepatic artery, urine from kidney to bladder: ureter
urea to the kidney: hepatic artery, urine from kidney to bladder: urethra
urea to the kidney: renal artery, urine from kidney to bladder: ureter
urea to the kidney: renal artery, urine from kidney to bladder: urethra

title: Question 9 (Page 93, #16)
question: Which structure produces the anti-diuretic hormone (ADH)?
explanation: When the osmotic potential in the blood vessels changes, the hypothalamus in the brain is stimulated to produce ADH.

title: Question 10 (Page 93, #17)
question: Which row correctly describes the mechanism of the anti-diuretic hormone (ADH)?
explanation: When water potential in the plasma is high, less ADH is released. This causes less water to be reabsorbed by the collecting ducts so urine volume increases and urine concentration decreases. When water potential in the plasma is low, more ADH is released. There is increased reabsorption of water in the nephrons so the urine collected would be more concentrated.

options.option_text: water potential in plasma: high, ADH release: decreased, Urine: dilute
water potential in plasma: high, ADH release: increased, Urine: concentrated
water potential in plasma: low, ADH release: decreased, Urine: concentrated
water potential in plasma: low, ADH release: increased, Urine: dilute

title: Question 1 (Page 94, #18)
question:
Which of these organ(s) is/are involved in the excretion of excess water?

&&img&& PAGE_94_Q18 &&img&&
explanation: The skin removes excess water in the form of sweat; the lung removes excess water in the form of water vapour during exhalation and the kidney removes excess water in the form of urine.

title: Question 2 (Page 94, #19)
question:
Which of these organ(s) is/are involved in the excretion of excess mineral salts?

&&img&& PAGE_94_Q19 &&img&&
explanation: The skin removes excess mineral salts as one of the components of sweat and the kidney removes excess mineral salts as one of the components of urine.

title: Question 3 (Page 94, #20)
question:
Which of these organ(s) is/are involved in the excretion of nitrogenous waste products?

&&img&& PAGE_94_Q20 &&img&&
explanation: The skin removes nitrogenous waste products as one of the components of sweat, although this is present in sweat in very minute amounts. The kidney is the main excretory organ of nitrogenous waste as one of the components of urine. Although the liver is involved in the formation of urea, it does not excrete nor remove the urea on its own.

title: Question 4 (Page 94, #21)
question:
Which of these organs is/are involved in the excretion of bile pigments from the breakdown of haemoglobin?

&&img&& PAGE_94_Q21 &&img&&
explanation: Bile pigments are broken down in the liver then transported to the intestines to be removed in the form of faecal discharge.

title: Question 5 (Page 94, #22)
question: What type of food should a person with kidney failure reduce his intake of?
explanation: High protein consumption will lead to increased urea concentration in the blood of a person with kidney failure as the kidneys are unable to process and remove the urea formed efficiently.

title: Question 6 (Page 94, #23)
question: What provides the force for ultrafiltration in the kidney tubules?
explanation: The contraction of the left ventricle creates a high hydrostatic blood pressure in the glomerulus that allows movement of small molecules from the blood into the Bowman's capsule.

title: Question 7 (Page 94, #24)
question:
When a person is running a marathon, which of the following is likely to occur?

&&img&& PAGE_94_Q24 &&img&&
explanation: During a marathon, the runner loses plenty of water in the form of sweat. This will stimulate the pituitary gland to release more ADH. The ADH will increase the reabsorption of water in the kidney tubules, resulting in a smaller volume of urine produced.

options.option_text: less amount of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secreted, less reabsorption of water from kidney tubule, more volume of urine produced
less amount of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secreted, more reabsorption of water from kidney tubule, less volume of urine produced
more amount of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secreted, less reabsorption of water from kidney tubule, more volume of urine produced
more amount of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secreted, more reabsorption of water from kidney tubule, less volume of urine produced

title: Question 8 (Page 94, #25)
question: Cells lining the kidney tubule have a high density of mitochondria. Why is this necessary?
explanation: Mitochondria are 'power houses' in a cell that release energy for cellular activities. Diffusion is a passive process that does not require energy, but active transport requires energy in order to move substances against a concentration gradient. During ultrafiltration, substances are moved from the blood into the kidney tubule due to the hydrostatic pressure difference between the afferent and efferent arterioles. This is a passive process that does not require energy. During selective reabsorption however, some substances will be transported from the nephron back into the blood capillaries against a concentration gradient and energy is therefore expended.

options.option_text: active transport of substances during selective reabsorption
active transport of substances during ultrafiltration
diffusion of substances during selective reabsorption

title: Question 9 (Page 94, #26)
question:
What substance will not be found in the dialysis fluid entering the dialysis machine?

&&img&& PAGE_94_Q26 &&img&&
explanation: Creatinine is a metabolic waste substance which should not be found in the dialysis fluid entering the machine so that a steep concentration gradient can be established. This enables creatinine waste in the patient's blood to diffuse out of the dialysis tubing more efficiently.

title: Question 10 (Page 94, #27)
question:
Which substance will not be found in the dialysis fluid leaving the dialysis machine?

&&img&& PAGE_95_Q28 &&img&&
explanation: A patient with kidney failure would have a high urea concentration in his blood, so blood flowing out from his vein would have a high urea concentration while the blood returning to his body via the vein would have a low urea concentration. The dialysis fluid entering the machine should have a low urea concentration to ensure optimal diffusion of urea out from the patient's blood into the dialysis fluid.

options.option_text: W: high, X: high, Y: low, Z: low
W: high, X: low, Y: low, Z: high

Which of the following comparisons is correct?

&&img&& PAGE_95_Q29 &&img&&
explanation: Dialysis fluid Y will need to have a lower concentration of urea than blood W. This sets up a concentration gradient that will enable urea to move out of the blood into the dialysis fluid, thus removing metabolic waste from the patient's blood.

options.option_text: Blood W will have more amino acids than blood X.
Blood W will have more red blood cells than blood X.
Dialysis fluid Y will have a lower concentration of glucose than blood W.

title: Question 3 (Page 95, #30)
question:
At which region is the concentration of urea the lowest?

&&img&& PAGE_95_Q30 &&img&&
explanation: The dialysis fluid introduced into the machine has no urea. This is to increase efficiency in removal of urea from the blood via diffusion.

title: Question 4 (Page 95, #31)
question:
What could substances P and Q be?

&&img&& PAGE_95_Q31 &&img&&
explanation: The dialysis tubing in a dialysis machine is partially permeable which means protein molecules in the blood are unable to move out from the patient's blood into the dialysis fluid. Carbon dioxide is not a useful substance to the patient, and thus will not be preserved in the dialysis fluid at a higher concentration than blood carbon dioxide levels. Hence, the best option for this question would be D.

title: Question 5 (Page 95, #32)
question:
Which of the following will decrease the concentration of urine? 

1 increased anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) 
2 increased consumption of water 
3 increased physical activity 
4 increased sweating
explanation: Increased ADH results in kidney tubules reabsorbing more water, thus, the urine becomes more concentrated. Increased physical activity will result in increased metabolism and therefore, more metabolic waste will be produced. This will cause increase in urea concentration in urine. Increased sweating will cause an overall drop in water potential of the blood plasma, which will trigger increased ADH release into the bloodstream, causing reduced urine production and therefore, urine is more concentrated. The only activity which decreases concentration of urea in the urine would be the increased consumption of water which raises the water potential in the blood plasma, which triggers less ADH to be secreted into the blood and hence, cause the nephrons to reabsorb less water. This causes more urine to be produced and thus the urea concentration is lower.

title: Question 6 (Page 95, #33)
question:
Which process, 1, 2, 3 or 4 represents deamination?

&&img&& PAGE_95_Q33 &&img&&

title: Question 1 (Page 96, #34)
question:
Which process occurs in the liver and kidney?

&&img&& PAGE_96_Q34 &&img&&
explanation: Deamination (1) occurs in the liver while the formation of urine (3) occurs in the kidney.

title: Question 3 (Page 96, #36)

explanation: In a healthy person, all the glucose should have been reabsorbed in the kidney tubules and there should be no glucose present in the urine at all.

title: Question 4 (Page 96, #37)
question:
A biomedical engineer was asked to improve the design of the dialysis machine to shorten the duration of a dialysis session which typically lasts for at least four hours. The engineer came up with the following suggestions: 

1 increase length and coiling of dialysis tubing 
2 increasing the rate of flow of dialysis fluid 
3 increase wall thickness of tubing containing blood 

Which of these recommendations will shorten the duration of dialysis session?
explanation: Increasing the length of tubing will lead to increase in surface area for a faster diffusion of urea into the dialysis fluid. Increasing the rate of flow of dialysis fluid will lead to maintenance of a high concentration gradient for a faster diffusion of urea. However, increasing the wall thickness of tubing for blood will result in slower rate of diffusion across the thicker wall.

title: Question 5 (Page 96, #38)

title: Question 6 (Page 96, #39)
question: Which of the following conclusions about the results is incorrect?
explanation: Proteins are broken down into amino acids. Excess amino acids are deaminated to form urea and excreted in the urine. So a person on a high protein diet will not have proteins found in his urine, but a higher concentration of urea. If proteins are found in the urine, it is usually an indication of the kidney's inability to filter substances in the blood optimally. Proteins are large molecules and should be retained within the glomerulus during ultrafiltration.

options.option_text: The patient with glucose present in the blood may have low insulin production.
A healthy individual who has a high protein diet will have proteins found in his urine.
The presence of alcohol in the urine shows that the patient's liver may not be working optimally.

title: Question 7 (Page 96, #40)

The quantity of substances in the urine of a healthy female is shown in the table below. A few hours after consumption of a meal comprising fish and chips and 800 ml of water, what will the likely changes in the quantity of her urine be?

&&img&& PAGE_96_Q40 &&img&&
explanation: Although the fish and chips are high in protein and carbohydrates, all the amino acids and glucose should be selectively reabsorbed by the kidney and will therefore be absent in the urine. The high salt content of the dish will lead to the excretion of more salt in the urine. Deamination of excess amino acids and metabolic processes taking place in the body will lead to an increase in the excretion of urea. Since she had drunk quite a significant amount of water in the meal, she will be excreting more water in her urine.

options.option_text: amino acids: increase, glucose: increase, salt: increase, urea: increase, water: increase
amino acids: increase, glucose: unchanged, salt: decrease, urea: unchanged, water: decrease
amino acids: unchanged, glucose: unchanged, salt: increase, urea: increase, water: increase
amino acids: unchanged, glucose: increase, salt: decrease, urea: increase, water: decrease

title: Question 1 (Page 97, #41)
question:
Which substance(s) in blood cannot pass through a dialysis membrane?

1 fibrinogen
2 glucagon
3 white blood cell
explanation: The dialysis membrane is partially permeable so large molecules cannot pass through. Fibrinogen is a plasma protein, while glucagon is a hormone. Both of these are too large to pass through the dialysis membrane. White blood cells are also very large and cannot pass through the dialysis membrane.

title: Question 2 (Page 97, #42)
question:

aorta → renal vein → vena cava → hepatic vein (lowest to highest urea amount)
renal vein → aorta → hepatic vein → vena cava (lowest to highest urea amount)

title: Question 1 (Page 98, #47)
question: On a warm and sunny day, which substance will be excreted by a green plant?
explanation: The green plant photosynthesises on a warm and sunny day to produce glucose and oxygen. The glucose is converted into starch and stored in the plant. Some of the oxygen will be used by the plant for respiration but the excess will diffuse out of the stomata.

title: Question 2 (Page 98, #48)
question:
Which of the following conclusions can be made from the diagram and table?

&&img&& PAGE_98_Q48 &&img&&

The total urea excreted in the cow and dromedary's urine is (volume × concentration of urea) 1120 g and 408 g respectively so option D is not true. options.option_text: The dromedary has a lower water consumption than the cow.

question:
What does the difference between the dromedary and the cow nephron suggest about their habitat?

&&img&& PAGE_98_Q49 &&img&&
explanation: The high urine output in the cow suggests that its habitat has no shortage of water. The low urine output in the dromedary suggests that its habitat has low availability of water.

title: Question 4 (Page 98, #50)
question:
What substance should not be found in fresh dialysis fluid?

&&img&& PAGE_98_Q50 &&img&&
explanation: Urea is a waste product and should not be found in the fresh dialysis fluid. This sets up a steeper concentration gradient which allows urea found in the patient's blood to diffuse more efficiently into the dialysis fluid.

title: Question 5 (Page 98, #51)
question:
Peritoneal dialysis is usually performed overnight while the patient is sleeping. Which of the following explains why peritoneal dialysis takes a longer time compared to haemodialysis methods where blood is drawn from a patient's arm into a dialysis machine?

&&img&& PAGE_98_Q51 &&img&&
explanation: The countercurrent exchange mechanism in the haemodialysis set-up helps to maintain a steep concentration gradient which increases the rate of diffusion of waste products from the patient's blood into the dialysis fluid. In contrast, the peritoneal dialysis method causes a build-up of waste products in the dialysis fluid over time, which then slows the rate of diffusion of waste products from the patient's blood into the dialysis fluid.

options.option_text: In haemodialysis, there is a pump which creates a force that moves the waste substances more efficiently from the blood into the dialysis fluid via active transport.
In haemodialysis, the direction of blood flow runs opposite to the direction of flow of the dialysis fluid, maintaining a steep concentration gradient.
In peritoneal dialysis, the lack of mitochondria in the patient's tissue results in less energy released to drive the diffusion of waste substances into the dialysis fluid.
The dialysis fluid in peritoneal dialysis has a higher concentration of urea compared to that in haemodialysis, so rate of diffusion is slower.

title: Question 1 (Page 99, #52)
question:

&&img&& PAGE_99_Q52 &&img&&
explanation: The results from the Benedict's test and biuret test indicate the presence of glucose and proteins, respectively, in the patient's urine. Patients with kidney failure may be unable to prevent plasma proteins in the glomerulus from filtering into the kidney tubules, hence, proteins will be found in the urine.

title: Question 2 (Page 99, #53)
question: Mangrove plants are adapted to survive in environments with high salinity and humidity. Which of the following is unlikely to be an excretory product of mangrove plants?
explanation: Carbon dioxide is an excretory product of respiration while oxygen is an excretory product of photosynthesis. Living in an environment with high salt content, much of the salts is taken in with the water by the roots and is excreted through their leaves. Most plants, including the mangrove plants, use the excess nitrogen and convert it into usable essential or non-essential amino acids that are stored. Most plants also do not have the necessary mechanisms to produce urea.

title: Question 3 (Page 99, #54)
question: Which of the following is an effect of aspirin on renal function?
explanation: The amount of nitrogenous waste (urea and creatinine) in the blood increases in the group of patients treated with aspirin, suggesting that less waste is being removed by the kidneys. The blood urea and creatinine concentrations show a decrease between week 2 and week 5 after the administering of the aspirin, indicating that the increase is not a permanent one.

options.option_text: decreases kidneys' ability to remove nitrogenous waste

title: Question 4 (Page 99, #55)
question: Which of the following does not explain why aspirin should not be administered to patients suffering from renal problems?
explanation: Filtration in the Bowman's capsule is based on size of molecules and not based on chemical composition. It is unlikely that aspirin would cause 'selective filtration' in the kidney tubules.

options.option_text: Aspirin causes the body cells to increase their metabolic activity.
Aspirin increases overall nitrogenous waste concentration in the blood.
Aspirin reduces the kidney's ability to filter nitrogenous waste from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule.
Aspirin causes the kidneys to reabsorb nitrogenous waste.

title: Question 5 (Page 99, #56)

explanation: The presence of microvilli and many mitochondria suggests that this cell is involved in absorption. The proximal convoluted tubule is a site of selective reabsorption while the Bowman's capsule is where ultrafiltration occurs. title: Question 1 (Page 100, #1)
question: What is the primary function of sweat?
explanation: Sweat helps to cool down the body when it is evaporated from the skin. Although some urea is dissolved in the sweat, the amount is negligible and the removal of excess urea is primarily performed by the kidneys.

title: Question 2 (Page 100, #2)
question:
Which of the following will cause an increase in human body temperature?

1 increased evaporation of sweat
2 reduced blood flow to the skin capillaries
3 shivering
explanation: Increased evaporation of sweat will cause a decrease in body temperature. Reduced blood flow to the skin capillaries will reduce heat loss by conduction, convection and radiation, thus increasing body temperature. Shivering causes the muscles to release more heat, so body temperature also increases.

title: Question 3 (Page 100, #3)
question: Which of these bodily processes does not require homeostatic control?
explanation: The constancy of body temperature, pH of tissue fluid and water potential of blood are all under the body's homeostatic control. The amount of food ingested is a voluntary reaction that is not subject to homeostatic control.

title: Question 4 (Page 100, #4)
question: Which is not an essential component of homeostatic control?
explanation: Although hormones may be involved in some processes of homeostatic control, it is not an essential component. For example, thermal regulatory mechanisms do not involve hormones.

title: Question 5 (Page 100, #5)
question: Which of these is not a corrective mechanism for elevated glucose levels in the blood?
explanation: When glucose levels are increased, more insulin is secreted and released into the bloodstream. Insulin increases the permeability of the cell membranes to glucose, causing glucose to be absorbed more quickly by cells. Insulin also causes the liver and muscles to convert more glucose into glycogen. Insulin also results in the increased oxidation of glucose during cellular respiration.

options.option_text: increased permeability of cell membranes to glucose

title: Question 6 (Page 100, #6)
question: Which of these is not a corrective mechanism for decreased water potential of blood?
explanation: The blood water potential, and not the urine concentration is being constantly monitored by the hypothalamus. When the water potential of blood is low, more ADH is released into the bloodstream. This causes more water to be reabsorbed by the kidney tubules, resulting in a lower volume of urine excreted. The lower volume of water in the urine causes the urine to have a higher concentration of solutes.

options.option_text: increased water reabsorption by the kidneys

title: Question 7 (Page 100, #7)
question:
Which of these rows shows an incorrectly paired stimulus-receptor combination?

&&img&& PAGE_100_Q7 &&img&&
explanation: Changes in the water potential of blood are detected by receptors found in the hypothalamus. This then stimulates the pituitary gland to increase or decrease anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) secretions into the blood.

options.option_text: blood glucose concentration - islets of Langerhans
water potential of blood - pituitary gland

title: Question 8 (Page 100, #8)
question:
When a person's body temperature decreases, which of the following corrective mechanisms will occur?

1 contraction of hair erector muscles
2 shivering
3 shunt vessels dilate
4 vasodilation of skin arterioles
explanation: The hair erector muscles contract, causing the hairs to 'stand'. This enables the trapping of a layer of air which serves to insulate against heat loss. Shivering causes the release of heat by the muscles to warm up the body. The dilation of shunt vessels cause less blood to flow towards the skin capillaries so less heat is lost at the skin surface. When a person's temperature decreases, the skin arterioles constrict, not dilate, so that less blood flows towards the skin capillaries, reducing heat loss.

title: Question 9 (Page 100, #9)

decreased water potential of blood - increased anti-diuretic (ADH) release

increased body temperature - increased skeletal muscle contractions

title: Question 1 (Page 101, #10)
question:
The diagram shows a schematic representation of the skin. Which of the labelled structures show the sweat gland and the thermoreceptor?

&&img&& PAGE_101_Q10 &&img&&
explanation: Thermoreceptors are located nearer the epidermis (topmost layers of the skin while pressure receptors (4) are located in the dermis layers. Sweat glands can be identified by their duct that connects to the skin surface.

title: Question 2 (Page 101, #11)
question:
Which of the labelled structures contains muscles that contract and/or relax to regulate body temperature?

&&img&& PAGE_101_Q11 &&img&&
explanation: The skin arterioles (3) contain muscles that contract or relax to decrease or increase the amount of blood flowing through the skin capillaries respectively. When the arterioles contract (constrict), less blood flows to the skin capillaries, so less heat is lost at the skin surface. When the arterioles dilate, more blood flows to the skin capillaries, so more heat is lost at the skin surface. This enables the skin arterioles to regulate body temperature.

title: Question 3 (Page 101, #12)
question:

3. On a hot day, the shunt vessels constrict so more heat can be lost by conduction, convection and radiation. 
4. Thermoregulation is under voluntary control by the brain.
explanation: Sweat is continuously being secreted. On cool days, the amount of sweat produced is in very small quantities and may evaporate almost immediately so a person does not feel it. Thermoregulation is a reflex action and not a voluntary action.

title: Question 4 (Page 101, #13)
question:
Which of the following organs are not involved in thermoregulation?

2. pituitary gland

explanation: The pituitary gland is involved in osmoregulation but not thermoregulation. Sebaceous glands secrete the oily substance, sebum, which acts as an antiseptic and prevents dehydration of the skin.

title: Question 5 (Page 101, #14)
question: Which of the following shows the correct corrective mechanism to the named stimulus?
explanation: When body temperatures are elevated, the shunt vessels constrict so more blood is carried to the skin capillaries and more heat is lost from the skin surface. stimulus: increased glucose concentration in blood, corrective mechanism: increased production of glucagon

sweat glands: more active, shunt vessels: constricted, skin arterioles: dilated

small mammals: higher rate of urea production, large mammals: lower rate of urea production
small mammals: more active sweat glands, large mammals: less active sweat glands

title: Question 8 (Page 101, #17)
question: Which of the following is not an effector of thermoregulation in humans?
explanation: The hypothalamus is the receptor that detects changes in the body temperature and initiates the reflex for thermoregulation.

title: Question 1 (Page 102, #18)

person is eating a hot bowl of soup noodles

title: Question 3 (Page 102, #20)
question:
Which of these changes occurs in an athlete's body while he is running a marathon?

title: Question 4 (Page 102, #21)
question:
Which homeostatic mechanisms are involved in the regulation of body temperature?

title: Question 2 (Page 103, #26)
