The graph shows how a person's core temperature varies over a period of time. During which time interval would the skin arterioles show the greatest increase in diameter?

&&img&& PAGE_103_Q27 &&img&&
explanation: The skin arterioles dilate the most when the body core temperature shows a great increase. This allows more blood to flow to the skin capillaries so heat can be lost at the skin surface.

title: Question 4 (Page 103, #28)
question:
The diagram shows blood vessels that are found under skin. X refers to the muscular wall of the vessel leading to the dense capillary network found under the skin. Which of the following events will lead to the contraction of muscles labelled X?

&&img&& PAGE_103_Q28 &&img&&
explanation: Contraction of muscle X (vasoconstriction) leads to a decrease in blood supply to the capillary network under the skin. This decreases heat loss and will happen only when exposed to cold temperatures. Listening to music will not affect vasodilation or vasoconstriction.

options.option_text: entering a very cold room without thermal wear
having a jogging session in the evening

title: Question 5 (Page 103, #29)
question:
The graph shows some changes in a person's body temperature. What could have happened at time periods X and Y to cause the change in the body temperature?

&&img&& PAGE_103_Q29 &&img&&
explanation: Exercise causes a person's body temperature to increase. When shunt vessels constrict, more blood flows towards the skin capillaries and more heat is lost at the skin surface via conduction, convection and radiation, causing the body temperature to decrease. Increased adrenaline and ADH release would have no effect on a person's body temperature. When sleeping, a person's metabolism rate is decreased and the body temperature usually decreases slightly.

options.option_text: X: exercise, Y: shunt vessels constrict
X: increased adrenaline release, Y: sweat glands become less active
X: increased anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) release, Y: skin arterioles dilate

title: Question 6 (Page 103, #30)
question:
The diagram shows how the body temperature of a person varies over a period of five days. What is the average temperature reading of the individual during these five days?

&&img&& PAGE_103_Q30 &&img&&
explanation: The sum of all the temperature readings divided by ten would give an average of 37.21°C. (37°C + 37.24°C + 37.48°C + 37.32 °C + 37.44°C + 37.24°C + 37.32°C + 37.04°C + 37.12°C + 36.88°C) ÷ 10 = 37.21°C

title: Question 1 (Page 104, #31)
question: During which time period would the person's skin arterioles show the smallest average diameter?
explanation: The skin arterioles would have the smallest average diameter when the body temperature is low. This prevents less blood flowing to the skin capillaries and therefore less heat is lost at the skin surfaces. The time period with the lowest average temperature would be option D with an average reading of 37.06°C.

options.option_text: between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. on day 1
between 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. on day 2
between 6 p.m. on day 3 and 6 a.m. on day 4
between 6 p.m. on day 4 and 6 a.m. on day 5

title: Question 2 (Page 104, #32)
question:
The diagram shows part of the skin under normal conditions and under condition X. What is condition X?

&&img&& PAGE_104_Q32 &&img&&
explanation: The skin under condition X shows secretion of sweat and dilated skin arterioles with increased blood flow to the skin capillaries. These evidences suggest that the body is trying to remove heat from its core.

title: Question 3 (Page 104, #33)
question:
The diagram shows a cross-section of a human skin. Which row correctly matches the labelled part with its function?

&&img&& PAGE_104_Q33 &&img&&
explanation: The sweat glands (T) excrete small amounts of urea and other nitrogenous compounds. The fat cells (U) provide a layer of insulation against cold conditions. Blood vessels (S) transport oxygen and nutrients to the skin, and at the same time remove carbon dioxide and other waste materials.

options.option_text: excretion: P, insulation: R, transport: P
excretion: R, insulation: U, transport: S
excretion: S, insulation: R, transport: P
excretion: T, insulation: U, transport: S

title: Question 4 (Page 104, #34)
question: A person takes a hot bath and her body temperature increases from 36.7°C to 37.4°C. Which of the following is not likely to occur during her hot bath?
explanation: As her body temperature increases, her skin arterioles in her face dilate so more blood travels to the skin capillaries and excess heat can be removed at the skin surface. Due to the increased lumen size, the blood pressure in her skin arterioles would decrease.

options.option_text: The blood pressure in her skin arterioles decreases.
The skin arterioles in her face constrict.

title: Question 5 (Page 104, #35)
question: Graves' disease is an autoimmune disease where the patient secretes excess thyroxine, resulting in increased metabolic rate in the body. Which is not a possible symptom of a person suffering from Graves' disease?
explanation: Patients suffering from Graves' disease have a higher body temperature due to increased metabolic activity. This causes them to have increased heart rates to transport heat away from the core towards the skin, so the heat can be removed by conduction, convection and radiation. They will also experience increased sweating to lower their body temperatures. As a result of their elevated body temperatures, they are less able to tolerate warm environments, so they have decreased heat tolerance.

title: Question 6 (Page 104, #36)
question:
Soldiers often train for extended periods under the hot sun. Which of the following are ways by which a soldier can prevent himself from feeling the effects of heatstroke? 

1 Drinking lots of warm water to stay hydrated 
2 Putting down their backpacks when possible to increase air circulation around their bodies 
3 Wearing lightweight cotton fabrics so air can reach their skin and cool them
explanation: Drinking warm water can cause the soldiers core temperatures to become elevated. They should drink cold water instead.

title: Question 7 (Page 104, #37)
question:
Humans, like most other mammals, are considered homoiotherms, where they are able to maintain a constant body temperature. Invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles and fishes are considered poikilotherms, where their body temperatures are able to vary depending on the temperatures of their surrounding environment.

Which of the following is not likely to be a physical feature of poikilothermic organisms?
explanation: Poikilothermic organisms have body temperatures that conform to that of their external environment so they are unlikely to have sweat glands that 'cool' them. Since they do not need to regulate their body temperatures, they will therefore lack dense networks of capillaries and nerve receptors under their skin.

options.option_text: lack of thermoreceptors in the skin

title: Question 1 (Page 105, #38)
question:
Humans, like most other mammals, are considered homoiotherms, where they are able to maintain a constant body temperature. Invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles and fishes are considered poikilotherms, where their body temperatures are able to vary depending on the temperatures of their surrounding environment.

The graph shows the relationship between environmental temperature and the body temperatures of organisms 1, 2, 3 and 4. Which graphs are likely to represent the body temperatures of a homoiotherm and a poikilotherm respectively?

&&img&& PAGE_105_Q38 &&img&&
explanation: Homoiotherms would have a constant body temperature independent of their environmental temperatures. Poikilotherms would have body temperatures that decrease and increase with environmental temperatures (ie. directly proportional relationship).

title: Question 2 (Page 105, #39)
question: Athletes cool down in temperate countries faster than in tropical countries, even when the ambient temperatures are the same. Which is the best explanation for this phenomenon?
explanation: With a lower humidity, the sweat evaporates faster from the skin of athletes, enabling more efficient heat loss at the skin surfaces.

options.option_text: Temperate countries have a lower humidity, enabling sweat to evaporate faster.
Temperate countries have lower oxygen concentrations in the air, so athletes have a higher breathing rate.
Temperate countries have wider diurnal temperature ranges, which cause increased production of sweat.
Temperate countries provide a higher optimum temperature for enzymes to work.

title: Question 3 (Page 105, #40)
question:
A man enters a hot sauna and stays there for about 30 minutes. Which of the following graphs best represents his skin temperature and rate of sweating during these 30 minutes?

&&img&& PAGE_105_Q40 &&img&&
explanation: The air in the sauna is warm, so the man's body temperature would increase as heat from the surrounding air is transferred to his body. In response to the increase in temperature, the homeostatic mechanism for thermoregulation kicks in. To remove some of the excess heat, his skin arterioles would dilate causing more blood to enter the skin capillaries—this causes an increase in his skin temperature. At the same time, his sweat glands would be more active, so more sweat would be produced. When the sweat evaporates, heat is removed and the temperature of the skin decreases.

options.option_text: Graph A showing temperature and sweating patterns over time
Graph B showing temperature and sweating patterns over time
Graph C showing temperature and sweating patterns over time
Graph D showing temperature and sweating patterns over time

title: Question 4 (Page 105, #41)
question:
Four test subjects had their blood glucose level monitored for 2.5 hours after they drank a can of sugary drink. Of the four test subjects, only one of them is a healthy individual. (Normal range for blood glucose levels is 72-99 mg 100 cm⁻³.) Which of them is most likely to be the healthy individual?

&&img&& PAGE_105_Q41 &&img&&
explanation: Person D's blood glucose levels are maintained within normal range, with an increase in glucose concentration immediately after having the drink before insulin was released to bring the blood glucose level back to normal. Both person A and B have blood glucose levels that are consistently higher than normal levels. Person C's glucose level decreases 3hr after the consumption of a high glucose drink. This suggests that C is likely to have issues absorbing glucose.

title: Question 1 (Page 106, #1)
question: What is the role of the intermediate neurons in the knee-jerk reflex?
explanation: The intermediate neurone, also known as the relay neurone, transmits nerve impulses from the sensory neurone to the motor neurone, and is found within the central nervous system.

options.option_text: carry electrical impulses within the spinal cord
communicate between the brain and the muscle effectors
detect pressure changes in the skin
pass impulses from the sensory neurones to the effectors

title: Question 2 (Page 106, #2)
question:
When a person is stung by a bee, the arm muscles contract to cause the arm to withdraw and a sharp pain is felt. Which part of the nervous system coordinates this arm movement and which part perceives the pain?

&&img&& PAGE_106_Q2 &&img&&
explanation: The central nervous system, comprising the brain and the spinal cord, co-ordinates responses to any stimulus. The spinal cord mostly co-ordinates responses that take place below the neck but the pain is always perceived by the brain.

options.option_text: coordinate arm movement: brain, pain perception: pain receptor
coordinate arm movement: motor neurone, pain perception: brain
coordinate arm movement: spinal cord, pain perception: pain receptor
coordinate arm movement: spinal cord, pain perception: brain

title: Question 3 (Page 106, #3)
question: A person notices that a ruler is falling from a table and reacts immediately to catch it before it reaches the floor. Which of the following correctly describes the route taken by the nerve impulses from the eye to the muscles of the hand?
explanation: The retina is the receptor that detects stimulus and produces a nerve impulse which then travels to the sensory neurone (optic nerve), then to the relay neurones in the brain, and spinal cord before it reaches the motor neurone to the muscle effectors.

options.option_text: optic nerve → retina → brain → spinal cord → motor neurone
optic nerve → retina → spinal cord → brain → motor neurone
retina → optic nerve → brain → spinal cord → motor neurone
retina → optic nerve → spinal cord → motor neurone

title: Question 4 (Page 106, #4)
question:
Which of the following best describes the difference between a sensory neurone and a motor neurone?

&&img&& PAGE_106_Q4 &&img&&
explanation: The detection of stimuli and initiation of nerve impulses are by receptors, not the sensory neurone. Both sensory and motor neurones are part of the peripheral nervous system.

options.option_text: sensory neurone: detects stimuli, motor neurone: does not detect stimuli
sensory neurone: part of central nervous system, motor neurone: part of peripheral nervous system
sensory neurone: produces nerve impulse, motor neurone: does not produce nerve impulse
sensory neurone: transmits impulse to relay neurone, motor neurone: receives impulse from relay neurone

title: Question 5 (Page 106, #5)
question:
The following is a list of the different components of the nervous system.
1 brain
2 motor neurone
3 receptor
4 relay neurone
5 sensory neurone
6 spinal cord

Which row correctly classifies the components into the central and peripheral nervous system?

&&img&& PAGE_106_Q5 &&img&&
explanation: The central nervous system is made up of only the brain, the spinal cord and the relay neurones that transmit impulses from the brain or spinal cord.

options.option_text: central nervous system: 1, 6, peripheral nervous system: 2, 3, 4, 5
central nervous system: 1, 3, 4, peripheral nervous system: 2, 5, 6
central nervous system: 1, 4, 6, peripheral nervous system: 2, 3, 5
central nervous system: 2, 4, 5, peripheral nervous system: 1, 3, 6

title: Question 6 (Page 106, #6)
question:
The following is a list of the different components of the nervous system.
1 brain
2 motor neurone
3 receptor
4 relay neurone
5 sensory neurone
6 spinal cord

Which components are involved in a spinal reflex?
explanation: In a spinal reflex, a receptor (3) detects a stimulus, generates a nerve impulse that travels along a sensory neurone (5) towards a relay neurone (4) in the spinal cord (6) then towards a motor neurone (2) towards an effector.

title: Question 1 (Page 107, #7)
question:
The following is a list of the different components of the nervous system.
1 brain
2 motor neurone
3 receptor
4 relay neurone
5 sensory neurone
6 spinal cord

Which components are involved in a cranial reflex?
explanation: In a cranial reflex, a receptor (3) detects a stimulus, generates a nerve impulse that travels along a sensory neurone (5) towards a relay neurone (4) in the brain (1) then towards a motor neurone (2) towards an effector.

title: Question 2 (Page 107, #8)
question:
The following is a list of the different components of the nervous system.
1 brain
2 motor neurone
3 receptor
4 relay neurone
5 sensory neurone
6 spinal cord

Which shows the nervous pathway for a voluntary action?
explanation: In most voluntary actions, the nerve impulse is generated by the brain and not the receptor. This nerve impulse then travels via the relay neurone towards the motor neurone and into the effectors. In most voluntary actions, the pathway would not include the roles of the receptor and the sensory neurone.

title: Question 3 (Page 107, #9)
question: Which of the following statements regarding a nervous response is true?
explanation: Communication in the nervous response is via electrical signals and chemical substances (neurotransmitters in the synapse). Nervous responses are very quick and usually localised to only one target organ.

options.option_text: Communication in the nervous response is via electrical signals only.
Impulses in the nervous response is transmitted by nerve cells.
It usually takes a long time before the effector responds to a stimulus during a nervous response.
Nervous responses usually affect more than one target organ.

title: Question 4 (Page 107, #10)
question: Which of these is not considered a reflex action?
explanation: The pinching of nose is a voluntary response that can be controlled by the will of the person.

options.option_text: pinching of nose in reaction to a bad smell
withdrawing of hand after touching a hot object

title: Question 5 (Page 107, #11)
question:
Three types of nerve cells are shown in the diagram below. In which order does a nerve impulse that is initiated by the receptor in a reflex response travel through?

&&img&& PAGE_107_Q11 &&img&&
explanation: The nerve impulse would travel through the sensory neurone (D) followed by the relay neurone (P) and lastly the motor neurone (R). The sensory neurone can be identified by the cell body, which is not found at the terminal end of the neurone but closer to the middle of the neurone. The motor neurone can be identified by the cell body at one of the terminal ends, together with a long axon. The relay neurone tends to have more branches as compared to the sensory or motor neurone.

title: Question 6 (Page 107, #12)
question:
In which region would the relay neurone be located?

&&img&& PAGE_107_Q12 &&img&&
explanation: The relay neurone is located in the grey matter of the spinal cord.

title: Question 7 (Page 107, #13)
question:
A person involved in a traffic accident got part of his spinal cord damaged and was unable to feel pain although he was able to move his muscles. Which region was likely to have been damaged in this accident?

&&img&& PAGE_107_Q13 &&img&&
explanation: Region A (dorsal root) contains the sensory neurone. The person was able to move, indicating that his brain was able to send signals via the relay and motor neurones to his muscles. Since he was unable to feel pain though, it would mean that signals from the receptor were not able to reach his brain. Since his leg neurone was intact, it would likely be his sensory neurone, that was located in the dorsal root was damaged.

title: Question 8 (Page 107, #14)
question: Which of the following statements regarding reflex actions is true?
explanation: In reflex actions, electrical signals will be sent to the brain. However, the brain often receives information simultaneously or after the effectors have received the information. Nerve impulses are initiated by the receptors and not the sensory neurone. In reflex actions, a stimulus to stimulate the receptors is always necessary.

options.option_text: No electrical signals are sent to the brain.
Spinal reflexes are controlled by the spinal cord.
The nerve impulse is initiated by the sensory neurone.
A stimulus may or may not be present.

title: Question 9 (Page 107, #15)
question: Epilepsy is a disease which causes the brain cells to produce abnormal, intermittent electrical discharges. Which of the following could be a resulting symptom in epileptic patients?
explanation: The production of electrical discharges would be conducted to muscle effectors causing muscle contractions.

title: Question 1 (Page 108, #16)
question:
What are the structures labelled P, Q and R?

&&img&& PAGE_108_Q16 &&img&&
explanation: Students need to be able to identify and name the structures involved in this reflex arc.

options.option_text: P: receptor, Q: sensory neurone, R: effector
P: sensory neurone, Q: relay neurone, R: motor neurone
P: sensory neurone, Q: spinal cord, R: effector
P: motor neurone, Q: relay neurone, R: sensory neurone

title: Question 2 (Page 108, #17)
question:
What is the structure in the skin that initiates this reflex reaction?

&&img&& PAGE_108_Q17 &&img&&
explanation: The heat from the hot pan is detected by temperature receptors in the skin of the finger which then generates a nerve impulse which is carried by the sensory neurone to the relay neurone, then to the motor neurone towards the effectors.

title: Question 3 (Page 108, #18)
question:
The nervous pathway that connects the receptor in the finger to the muscle in the arm is 1.2 metres long. If an electrical impulse travels at approximately 60 metres per second, what is the estimated time interval between the stimulus and the response?

&&img&& PAGE_108_Q18 &&img&&
explanation: Time = distance/Speed. Time taken therefore equals 1.2/80 = 0.015 seconds

title: Question 4 (Page 108, #19)
question:
A student studied the reflex arc pathway and made the following statements: 
1 Part A can be the sweat glands found in the skin. 
2 Part B converts pain signals detected in part A into nervous impulse. 
3 Part C can be found in the central nervous system. 
4 There is a conversion of nervous impulse into chemical signals between parts D and E. 
5 If part D is damaged, part E will not contract. 

Which statements made by the student are correct?

&&img&& PAGE_108_Q19 &&img&&
explanation: C represents the relay neurones which are found in the brain and spinal cord. Conversion of electrical impulse into chemical signals takes place at the synapse found between D and E. If the motor neurone (D) is damaged, signals cannot be sent to the effector muscles to contract (E). The sweat gland is not able to detect any stimulus thus option 1 is incorrect. It is the detector (A) that generates the nervous impulse and not the sensory neurone (B).

title: Question 5 (Page 108, #20)
question:
What are the names of the labelled parts?

&&img&& PAGE_108_Q20 &&img&&
explanation: The diagram shows a motor neurone. The axon of a motor neurone is much longer than the highly branched dendron. The myelin sheath is a fatty coat that encloses the axon and the gaps in between adjacent myelin sheaths are the nodes of Ranvier.

options.option_text: 1: axon, 2: myelin sheath, 3: node of Ranvier
1: axon, 2: node of Ranvier, 3: myelin sheath
1: dendron, 2: myelin sheath, 3: node of Ranvier
1: dendron, 2: node of Ranvier, 3: myelin sheath

title: Question 1 (Page 109, #21)
question: The trigeminal nerve in humans connects the teeth and parts of the facial skin to the brain. A dentist injects some local anaesthetics into an area near the trigeminal nerve causing the patient to feel numb in the area and not be able to smile. Based on this data, which of the following conclusions is correct?
explanation: The numbness felt by the patient indicates that impulses from the pain receptors are not transmitted to the brain, so the sensory neurones are affected. The inability to smile indicates that impulses from the brain are not transmitted to the facial muscles, so the motor neurone is also affected.

options.option_text: The trigeminal nerve carries messages from the brain to the teeth then to the skin.
The trigeminal nerve contains only motor neurones.
The trigeminal nerve contains only sensory neurones.
The trigeminal nerve contains sensory and motor neurones.

title: Question 2 (Page 109, #22)
question:
A person touches a hot frying pan by accident. She cannot feel the pain but moves her hand away once she notices the incident. At which point in this nervous pathway was the Botox injection applied?

&&img&& PAGE_109_Q22 &&img&&
explanation: If the person can still move, it means that signals from the brain can still be transmitted to the effectors via the relay neurone (Z) and the motor neurone (Y). But since she cannot feel the pain, it means that signals from the pain receptor are not able to reach the brain via the sensory nerve (X).

title: Question 3 (Page 109, #23)
question:
Another person touches the same hot frying pan by accident. He feels the sensation of pain, but is unable to withdraw his hand. At which point in his nervous pathway was the Botox injection applied?

&&img&& PAGE_109_Q23 &&img&&
explanation: The person can feel pain, which means that signals from the receptor is able to reach the brain via the sensory nerve (X) and the relay neurone in the spinal cord (Z). Nevertheless, since he cannot move his hand, it means that signals from the brain cannot reach his muscles (effectors) via the hand, so likely his motor nerve (Y) has been temporarily paralysed by the Botox injection.

title: Question 4 (Page 109, #24)
question:
What is the name and function of the damaged structures in the nerves of MS patients?

&&img&& PAGE_109_Q24 &&img&&
explanation: The diagram shows a motor neurone with damaged myelin sheath which acts as the protective coat of fatty substances that encloses many nerve cells and insulates the axon.

options.option_text: myelin sheath - decrease rate of electrical transmission
nodes of Ranvier - decrease rate of electrical transmission

title: Question 5 (Page 109, #25)
question: Which of the following is not a possible symptom of MS?
explanation: Options A, B and C are effects of nervous control so MS patients may be affected in these areas. Damages to the myelin sheath can affect the MS patients' co-ordination, movement, sensation, vision, etc., depending on the specific location of the damage. Red blood cell production is not co-ordinated by the nervous system so its production will not be affected in MS patients.

title: Question 1 (Page 110, #26)
question:
What are the identities of neurones X and Y?

&&img&& PAGE_110_Q26 &&img&&
explanation: A sensory neurone has a long dendron while a motor neurone has multiple dendrons (as well as dendrites). A sensory neurone also has a much shorter axon compared to the motor neurone. In addition, the cell body of a sensory neurone is not at the terminal end, while the cell body of a motor neurone is usually at the terminal end.

options.option_text: neurone X: motor, neurone Y: relay
neurone X: motor, neurone Y: sensory
neurone X: relay, neurone Y: sensory
neurone X: sensory, neurone Y: motor

title: Question 2 (Page 110, #27)
question:
In which direction are nerve impulses transmitted in neurones X and Y?

&&img&& PAGE_110_Q27 &&img&&
explanation: Neurone X is a motor neurone and the dendritic end is at Q while the axonal end is at P. Impulses on neurone X therefore transmit from Q to P. Neurone Y is a sensory neurone and the axon of sensory neurones are usually shorter than the dendrons. Impulses on neurone Y therefore transmit from S to R.

options.option_text: neurone X: P to Q, neurone Y: R to S
neurone X: P to Q, neurone Y: S to R
neurone X: Q to P, neurone Y: R to S
neurone X: Q to P, neurone Y: S to R

title: Question 3 (Page 110, #28)
question: What is the role of synapses in nervous transmission?
explanation: Synapses relay chemical messages between the axon of one neurone and the dendron of an adjacent neurone.

options.option_text: communicate between the brain and the spinal cord
communicate between the central nervous system and peripheral nervous system

title: Question 4 (Page 110, #29)
question: Which of the following statements about neurones is not true?
explanation: Neurones have a high density of mitochondria as a lot of energy is needed by these to transmit electrical impulses and to form neurotransmitters at the synaptic junctions.

options.option_text: Neurones have a low density of mitochondria so that there is less resistance in the transmission of the electrical impulse.
Sensory neurones always conduct impulses from the receptors to the relay neurones and not the other direction.
The cell bodies of the motor neurones are found in the grey matter of the spinal cord.
When a cluster of neurones are bundled together, they form a nerve.

title: Question 5 (Page 110, #30)
question:
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is a neuromuscular degenerative disease that causes motor neurones to gradually die, resulting in progressive loss of muscle mass. In which region of the spinal cord is SMA likely to affect?

&&img&& PAGE_110_Q30 &&img&&
explanation: Motor neurones are found in the anterior horn of the spinal cord (region D – ventral root) while sensory neurones are found in the posterior horn (region C – dorsal root). Region A shows the white matter where the nerve fibres of neurones are generally located and region B shows the grey matter, where the cell bodies of neurones are generally located.

title: Question 6 (Page 110, #31)
question:
The axons of motor neurones are insulated by a material known as myelin—multiple layers of phospholipids coated around the nerve fibre. The myelin is produced by Schwann cells. Which of the following organelles would be very active in a myelin-producing Schwann cell?

1 centrioles
2 endoplasmic reticulum
3 Golgi apparatus
4 plasma membrane

&&img&& PAGE_110_Q31 &&img&&
explanation: Lipids are produced by the endoplasmic reticulum which are then packaged by the Golgi apparatus to be modified into phospholipids. The centrioles are active during cell division and the plasma membrane's activity does not increase during myelin production since the myelin produced is used within the growing Schwann cell to wrap around the axon fibre.

title: Question 1 (Page 111, #1)
question:
Which of the labelled structures are involved in the pupil reflex?

&&img&& PAGE_111_Q1 &&img&&
explanation: In the pupil reflex, the circular and radial muscles in the iris (T) work together to control the size of the pupil (S) in response to light intensity.

title: Question 2 (Page 111, #2)
question:
Which of the labelled structures are involved in the accommodation reflex?

&&img&& PAGE_111_Q2 &&img&&
explanation: In the accommodation reflex, the ciliary muscles found in the ciliary body (P) work antagonistically with the suspensory ligaments (U) to control the curvature of the lens (Q).

title: Question 3 (Page 111, #3)
question: At which of the following parts of the eye would there be the greatest refraction of light?
explanation: There is greatest refraction of light at the cornea as light is passing from a gaseous medium (air) to a solid medium (cornea). Since the material density difference is greatest between gas and solid, the refraction would be greatest.

title: Question 4 (Page 111, #4)
question:
Which of the labelled structures contain muscles that control the amount of light entering the eye?

&&img&& PAGE_111_Q4 &&img&&
explanation: The circular and radial muscles in the iris (A) control the size of the pupil (B). The pupil itself is merely an aperture and does not contain muscles.

title: Question 5 (Page 111, #5)
question:
Which of the labelled structures protects the eye from mechanical damage?

&&img&& PAGE_111_Q5 &&img&&
explanation: The sclera (C) is a tough, white outer covering of the eyeball that has a protective function.

title: Question 6 (Page 111, #6)
question: Which row correctly identifies the initiator of the accommodation reflex and the effectors?
explanation: The retina is the receptor and initiates a nerve impulse in response to a stimulus. The ciliary muscle and suspensory ligaments are attached to the motor end plate of the motor neurone and respond in order to change the thickness of the lens.

options.option_text: optic nerve initiates reflex, ciliary muscle, suspensory ligaments as effectors
optic nerve initiates reflex, lens as effectors
retina initiates reflex, ciliary muscle, suspensory ligaments as effectors
retina initiates reflex, lens as effectors

title: Question 7 (Page 111, #7)
question: Which of the following changes will be expected when the ciliary muscles of a person contract?
explanation: When the ciliary muscles contract, the suspensory ligaments would become slackened, reducing their pull on the lens, causing it to become thicker. This would then allow the person to see nearby objects clearly.

options.option_text: The thickness of the lens decreases.
The person can see nearby objects more clearly.
The diameter of the pupil increases.

title: Question 1 (Page 112, #8)
question: Which of the following is not a characteristic of the image of an object formed on the retina?
explanation: The object distance is usually longer than the image distance. The eye is not able to focus objects that have a short object distance due to the limit on how thick and convex the eye lens can become.

options.option_text: equal distance from object to lens
smaller in size than actual object

title: Question 2 (Page 112, #9)
question: Which part of the eye supplies oxygen and nutrients to the eyeball?
explanation: The choroid is highly vascularised, so oxygen and nutrients in the blood is transported to the eyeball via the choroid, and the metabolic wastes are removed via the choroid too. Choroid is pigmented black to prevent internal reflection of light.

title: Question 3 (Page 112, #10)
question:
Which part(s) of the eye help to keep it firm?

1 aqueous humour
2 cornea
3 retina
4 scelera
5 vitreous humour
explanation: The aqueous and vitreous humours contain fluids that maintain hydrostatic pressure to keep the eyeball firm.

title: Question 9 (Page 112, #16)

explanation: When the student was doing her worksheet, the lens in her eye would be thicker and more convex to increase refraction of light. When she looked up at her teacher, the lens would become thinner and less convex as the teacher, who was standing in front of the class, was further away. lens shape: thinner, suspensory ligaments: become taut

Paul is driving along a coastal road on a midday afternoon. He then enters a tunnel. Which row shows the size of his pupils on the road and in the tunnel?

&&img&& PAGE_113_Q18 &&img&&
explanation: Along the coastal road on a midday afternoon, the surroundings would be very bright so Paul's pupils would constrict in order to limit the amount of light entering his eyes. In the tunnel, the surroundings are much dimmer so Paul's pupils would dilate in order to allow more light to enter his eyes.

options.option_text: along coastal road: small pupil, in the tunnel: small pupil
along coastal road: small pupil, in the tunnel: large pupil

explanation: The cinema is dark so the radial muscles of the iris would contract while the circular muscles would relax in order to dilate the pupil, allowing more light into the eye. The screen is far away, so the ciliary muscles would relax, pulling the suspensory ligaments to become taut in order to make the lens in the eye thinner and less convex to focus the distant image onto the retina.

circular muscles: contract, radial muscles: relax, ciliary muscles: relax, suspensory ligaments: taut
circular muscles: relax, radial muscles: contract, ciliary muscles: contract, suspensory ligaments: slack

explanation: The clarity of vision at X is zero, suggesting that there are no photoreceptors present at region X, thus X must be the blind spot where the optic nerve is found. In long-sightedness, the image formed is focused in a region behind the retina so the person also sees a blurry image.

title: Question 4 (Page 114, #25)
question: Albinism is a genetic condition where the person cannot produce melanin. Melanin is a tinted pigment which is found in the skin, hair and irises, and protects individuals from ultraviolet (UV) radiation. Which of the following is not a likely symptom associated with albinism?
explanation: The absence of melanin in the skin results in reduced protection from UV radiation so the person suffering from albinism (the albinos) can get sunburnt more easily. The absence of the dark pigment also gives albinos a pale appearance—mostly with whitish skin and hair, and pinkish-coloured irises. Light from the environment enters their eyes more easily through the pale-coloured irises and can cause increased sensitivity of the retina to light.

options.option_text: sensitivity of the retina to light

title: Question 5 (Page 114, #26)
question:
Marianne is sitting by the beach during sunset and observes several events happening around her. The changes in the thickness of the lens in her eyes are shown in the graph below. The events observed are as follows: 1 watching her friends walking slowly towards her 2 her attention is being caught by a loud warning horn of a passing ship 3 seeing a fly landing on her hand and waving it away 4 enjoying the view of the setting sun Which of these events are correctly matched with the periods P, Q, R and S in the graph?

&&img&& PAGE_114_Q26 &&img&&
explanation: Focusing on close objects causes Marianne's lens to thicken while focusing on objects that are far (≥7m) causes her lens to flatten and become thinner. Both P and R indicate that Marianne is focusing on objects that are close to her. However, the object in P must be much closer as the thickness of the lens increases the most, thus should be her seeing the fly landing on her hand. Period R will be her watching her friends walking closer towards her. Period Q shows her lens flattening rapidly as she focuses on a distant object looking at a closer object. This must have been the loud horn of the passing ship. As the sun is setting far away at the horizon, her lens will remain flattened as she observes the sunset for an extended period of time.

title: Question 1 (Page 115, #1)

title: Question 2 (Page 115, #2)

2 low water potential of blood

explanation: Adrenaline causes an increased conversion of glycogen into glucose, thereby raising blood glucose concentrations. Adrenaline also increases heart rate. Adrenaline has no effect on the water potential of blood.

title: Question 3 (Page 115, #3)

&&img&& PAGE_115_Q3 &&img&&

explanation: Endocrine glands produce secretions that are secreted directly into the blood stream. Glucagon and oestrogen are hormones produced by the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas and ovary respectively and these hormones are transported by the blood stream to the target organs. Amylase and bile are secreted and transported away by ducts. Amylase is secreted together with saliva into the salivary duct while bile is secreted into the bile duct.

title: Question 5 (Page 115, #5)

&&img&& PAGE_115_Q5 &&img&&

endocrine secretions: insulin, glucagon; exocrine secretions: amylase, trypsin

title: Question 6 (Page 115, #6)

title: Question 7 (Page 115, #7)
question: People who suffer from type 1 diabetes are unable to produce sufficient insulin. Which of the following is not a symptom associated with type 1 diabetes?
explanation: Glucose cannot be stored by the body, so people with type 1 diabetes have a high blood glucose concentration. The blood glucose concentration can be too high for the kidney to completely reabsorb all the glucose so some is excreted in the urine. Without insulin to convert glucose into glycogen, type 1 diabetics will also have low glycogen reserves and usually a low BMI as the body resorts to using fat for energy.

options.option_text: high glucose storage in body cells
low glycogen reserves in the body
low BMI as the body oxidises fats to release energy

title: Question 1 (Page 124, #31)
question:
Four women, Jane, Kate, Lynn and Meg had their blood progesterone levels monitored for a month after their first day of menstruation. The table shows their blood progesterone levels through the month. Based on the data given in the table above, which one of the women is likely to be pregnant?

&&img&& PAGE_124_Q31 &&img&&
explanation: Jane's progesterone level increases through the month, suggesting that the corpus luteum in her ovaries continues to secrete progesterone to maintain the thickened uterine lining for the embryo to embed itself in. This shows that Jane is likely to be pregnant. As for Kate and Lynn, their progesterone levels increase from day 5 all the way through to day 20. After day 20, their progesterone levels show a sharp decrease, indicating that no fertilisation occurred and menstruation started instead. Meg's progesterone level is constantly low with little fluctuation. This suggests that Meg could be a much older woman who is undergoing or has undergone menopause, so progesterone levels are generally low.

explanation: The blood group of the foetus may differ from that of the mother. Mixing of the two blood systems may result in the antibodies in the mother's blood to agglutinate the red blood cells of the foetus, which can be dangerous to both mother and the foetus. Protective antibodies from the mother may be allowed to diffuse through the placenta into the foetus to provide immunity to certain diseases. To maintain the blood pressure of the foetus, which is higher than the maternal blood pressure

&&img&& PAGE_128_Q50 &&img&&

explanation: Offspring of sexual reproduction receives a mixture of genes from parents while offspring of asexual reproduction is genetically identical to the parent. title: Question 2 (Page 129, #2)
question:
Which of the following describes the similarities between a pollen grain and a sperm cell? 
1 Both of them are formed by meiosis 
2 Both of them are motile 
3 Both of them carry the Y chromosome 
4 Both of them provide all the organelles needed for the zygote to develop
explanation: All gametes are formed by meiosis. However, only the sperm is motile (able to move) due to the presence of the tail (flagellum). title: Question 1 (Page 134, #35)
question:

Further research also showed that the physical characteristics of the flowers blooming in summer and the flowers blooming in winter can be slightly different.

The flowers blooming in summer are found to have a higher chance of developing into fruits as compared to those blooming in winter. Which of the following reasons help explain the observations made by the botanist?
explanation: Larger number of pollen produced and presence of more insects increase the chances of pollination to occur, leading to more fruits being formed. As the flower relies on insects for pollination, it is less reliant on wind for pollination to occur, thus (3) will not be a likely reason.

title: Question 3 (Page 134, #37)
question:
A fruit farmer decided to plant three papaya trees in a greenhouse. In an attempt to improve the annual fruit harvest, he provided an ideal climate for the trees all year round. Which of the above reasons could explain the lack of fruits being produced by these trees?

1 The enclosed greenhouse lacked wind or insect pollinators to pollinate the flowers
2 The three trees planted had unisexual male flowers
3 The trees require periods of cold winter temperartures to encourage development of fruit from flowers
explanation: Papaya trees are tropical fruit trees that do not grow well in cold regions, thus (3) is not possible. Papaya trees may produce unisexual flowers. A tree that produces only flowers with male reproductive parts will not be able to produce fruit. As the papaya tree requires pollinators such as insects or birds, the lack of such pollinators will make pollination impossible and thus, no fruits will be produced in an enclosed area such as a greenhouse.

title: Question 4 (Page 134, #38)
question:

The thrum flowers have short styles and long stamens while the pin flower bears flowers with long styles and short stamens. An observer made some statements regarding the two types of buckwheat flowers. Which of the above statements are likely to be correct?

1 A disease that kills buckwheat plants is less likely to eradicate populations with pin flowers compared to populations with thrum flowers
2 Buckwheat plants with pin flowers require less water to survive than those with thrum flowers
3 Buckwheat populations with thrum flowers show more genetic variation compared to populations with pin flowers
4 Self pollination is more likely to occur in thrum flowers than pin flowers

explanation: Plants with thrum flowers are more likely to self-pollinate due to the higher possibility of pollen from their own stamen landing on their own stigma, producing populations with less genetic diversity. Since pin flowers undergo cross-pollination more often, their offspring are genetically less similar and are thus likely to be eradicated by a disease as some individuals may have developed immunity. The amount of water needed for the plant to survive is not affected by the type of pollination.

title: Question 1 (Page 140, #36)

title: Question 2 (Page 140, #37)
question:

&&img&& PAGE_140_Q37 &&img&&
explanation: DNA replication occurs in the interphase, before the start of prophase. title: Question 3 (Page 140, #38)
question: 'Gemcitabine' is a drug used to treat patients with pancreatic or lung cancers. Gemcitabine works by inhibiting the action of DNA polymerase, an enzyme that is needed for DNA replication. During which stage of the cell cycle will Gemcitabine have an effect on?

title: Question 4 (Page 140, #39)

The diagram shows a pair of homologous chromosomes undergoing meiosis. G, g, H and h refer to the different alleles found in the chromosomes. At which stage of meiosis is the above diagram likely to be taken from?

&&img&& PAGE_140_Q39 &&img&&

title: Question 5 (Page 140, #40)
question: Assuming that crossing over does occur, which of the following is not a possible combination of alleles present in the resulting gametes formed after meiosis has occurred?
explanation: The G and g alleles are swapped during the crossing over. This results in the formation of chromosomes containing the allele combination of gH, gh, Gh and gH. A chromosome containing GH alleles exists before crossing over occurred, however after crossing over, none of the resulting chromosomes will have the GH allele combination.

explanation: Since Colchicine stops the mitotic process at metaphase, no cell will be in anaphase or telophase. C is incorrect as the cells are undergoing mitosis instead of meiosis, thus there will not be any homologous pairing of chromosomes.

The chromosomes of most cells are lined up as pairs of homologous chromosomes.
The chromosomes of most of the cells are split into sister chromatids.

title: Question 2 (Page 141, #43)
question: In which stage of mitosis is there an error in the number of chromosomes or chromatids in a human cell?
explanation: In prophase and metaphase, the sister chromatids of the 46 chromosomes have not been separated, thus the cell has only 46 chromosomes. However, in anaphase and telophase, the sister chromatids have been separated but the cell has not undergone cytokinesis to be split into two cells yet. Thus, there should be 92 chromosomes instead of 46 during and after anaphase.

title: Question 3 (Page 141, #44)
question: In which stage of meiosis is there an error in the number of chromosomes in a human cell?
explanation: In meiosis II, the homologous chromosomes have already been separated, leading to the reduction of chromosomes from 46 to 23. In prophase II and metaphase II, there should be 23 chromosomes as the sister chromatids have not been separated yet. However, the number of chromosomes doubles from 23 to 46 as the sister chromatids separate during anaphase II and are counted as two separate daughter chromosomes.

title: Question 4 (Page 141, #45)

&&img&& PAGE_141_Q45 &&img&&

options.option_text: DNA replication has occurred for the immature egg cell.
Independent assortment of homologous chromosomes has occurred in the immature egg cell.
The immature egg cell has haploid number of chromosomes.
The sister chromatids of the chromosomes have been separated.

title: Question 2 (Page 142, #48)
question: Fruit farmers often use triploid plants to grow seedless grapes. The cells of triploid plants contain 3n chromosomes instead of the usual 2n chromosomes. Which of the following reasons explains why triploid plants often produce grapes that are seedless?

Presence of an extra set of chromosomes might prevent the formation of flowers.

title: Question 1 (Page 149, #42)
question:
A biotechnologist tried to produce transgenic E. coli bacteria that were capable of producing human insulin. If different restriction enzymes are used to cut the human DNA and the bacterial plasmid, the resulting DNA fragments containing the insulin gene and the bacterial plasmids will not have complementary 'sticky ends' and will not join together to form a functional plasmid. He used different restriction enzymes to cut the insulin gene from human DNA and to cut the bacterial plasmid.

explanation: The drastic decrease in the cockroach population proves that majority of the cockroaches does not have the insecticide resistance gene in the beginning. options.option_text: a chance mutation conferring resistance to the insecticide happened in a few cockroaches.
all the cockroaches having a gene that conferred resistance to the insecticide.
some cockroaches acquiring the gene that confers resistance to the insecticide by feeding on some of the bees.
some cockroaches mating with the bees that have insecticide-resistance genes to produce offspring that are resistant to the insecticide.

title: Question 2 (Page 152, #56)
question:
'Mitochondrial disease' is caused by non-functional mitochondria that lead to muscle weakness, blindness and heart failure. The mutated gene that leads to the production of non-functional mitochondria is found in the DNA in the mitochondria itself, and not the DNA in the nucleus.

Using the following cells, a cloning procedure can be done to produce an embryo with the original nuclear DNA of the mother's ovum, but without the mutated DNA in the mitochondria: 

(1) mother's ovum with the mutated mitochondrial DNA 
(2) donor's ovum with normal mitochondrial DNA 
(3) father's sperm. 
What will the procedure needed to produce an embryo with the original nuclear DNA of the mother's ovum without the mutated mitochondria DNA be?
explanation: Since the mutated gene is found in the mitochondria of the mother, the mother's nuclear DNA should be removed and placed into the nucleus of the donor's ovum before being fertilised by the father's sperm. The embryo will then have the DNA of both the mother and father, but the normal mitochondrial DNA from the donor's ovum. This prevents the embryo from developing into a baby with mitochondrial disease.

step 1: remove mitochondrial DNA from mother's ovum, step 2: remove nuclear DNA from donor's ovum, step 3: insert mother's mitochondrial DNA into donor's ovum, step 4: fertilise donor's ovum with father's sperm
step 1: remove nuclear DNA from father's sperm, step 2: remove nuclear DNA from donor's ovum, step 3: insert father's nuclear DNA into donor's ovum, step 4: fertilise donor's ovum with mother's ovum
step 1: remove nuclear DNA from mother's ovum, step 2: remove nuclear DNA from donor's ovum, step 3: insert mother's nuclear DNA into donor's ovum, step 4: fertilise donor's ovum with father's sperm

explanation: Every three nucleotides in a DNA strand form a codon and every codon contains information for one amino acid during translation. Since the ratio of codons : amino acids is 1:1, the BRCA1 protein would contain 27 063 amino acids.

title: Question 1 (Page 153, #1)
question: What is the relationship between a gene and an allele?
explanation: A gene is a sequence of nucleotides in a chromosome, coding for a particular protein, which will be packaged to fulfil a certain function. For example, the gene coding for the human blood group codes for an enzyme that alters the proteins found on the surface of red blood cells. The gene coding for blood group type in humans has three distinct alleles—IA, IB and i°. The combination of two alleles inherited from parents will determine the blood group of the individual.

options.option_text: An allele codes for a particular characteristic or a protein while a gene is one of the many forms of the same allele.
An allele is the rod-like structure visible in the nucleus during cell division while a gene is one of the many forms of the same allele.
A gene codes for a particular characteristic or a protein while an allele is one of the many forms of the same gene.
A gene is the rod-like structure visible in the nucleus during cell division while an allele is one of the many forms of the same gene.

title: Question 2 (Page 153, #2)
question: Which of the following statements is not true?
explanation: Not all individuals have homozygous alleles in the same gene loci. Some individuals may have heterozygous alleles where one allele represents the dominant trait and the other allele represents the recessive trait.

options.option_text: Alleles of the same gene can be found in the same gene loci of homologous chromosomes.
Alleles of the same gene must not be homozygous.
Homologous chromosomes have the same sequence of gene loci.
Sister chromatids have the same sequence of gene loci.

title: Question 3 (Page 153, #3)
question: What is the relationship between a gene and a chromosome?
explanation: A chromosome comprises a double stranded DNA molecule wrapped around histone proteins. The DNA molecule consists of a continuous string of nucleotides. A gene consists of a sequence of nucleotides within this DNA molecule. Multiple genes can be found on the same chromosome, each occupying a specific position on the chromosome known as the gene locus.

options.option_text: A chromosome consists of many genes arranged in a particular sequence.
A gene is an alternative form of the chromosome.
A gene codes for a protein known as a chromosome.
Many chromosomes can be found in a gene.

title: Question 4 (Page 153, #4)
question: A phenotype is determined by
explanation: A phenotype is the expressed trait of an organism that can be affected by the genotype and the effects of its environment.

title: Question 5 (Page 153, #5)
question: If allele T is the dominant allele for cows with straight tails while the allele t is the recessive allele for cows with curly tails, what genotype will a pure bred cow with straight tails have?
explanation: A pure bred organism is homozygous for a trait, thus the genotype should be TT in this case.

title: Question 6 (Page 153, #6)
question: In fruit flies, the allele for red eye, R is dominant and the allele for brown eye, r is recessive. A red-eyed fly was mated with a brown-eyed fly. A total of 120 of the offspring had red eyes and the rest had brown eyes. How many brown-eyed offspring were likely to have been produced?
explanation: The red-eyed fly could be a homozygous dominant (RR) or heterozygous (Rr) since allele R is dominant for red eye. However, in this case, if the red-eyed fly was homozygous dominant, all offspring would have the dominant allele R and would therefore result in no brown-eyed offspring, which was not in any of the options given. Thus, the red-eyed fly must be a heterozygous individual whereby mating with a homozygous recessive brown-eyed fly would result in half of the total number of the offspring being homozygous recessive brown-eyed.

title: Question 7 (Page 153, #7)
question: In sheep, allele W, which codes for white wool is dominant over allele w, which codes for the recessive black wool. If a homozygous white sheep mates with a homozygous black sheep, what will be the likely percentage of offspring with black wool?
explanation: This cross will result in all of the offspring being heterozygous (Ww). Since W is the dominant allele that codes for white wool, all offspring will have white wool and none will have black wool.

title: Question 8 (Page 153, #8)

explanation: To find out the genotype of a plant, it must be test crossed with a homozygous recessive organism of the same species. Thus, plant Y should be homozygous recessive with the genotype tt.

title: Question 1 (Page 160, #51)
question:
Paternal lineage can be studied by tracing the Y chromosome of an individual. The Y chromosome is passed down from a father to his son down many generations.

Pete obtained the DNA of his paternal great-grandfather and proceeded to do the paternal lineage test where his Y chromosome and his great-grandfather's Y chromosome were analysed and compared. To his surprise, both Y chromosomes were not an exact match as 5% of the genetic material of his Y chromosomes differed from that of his great-grandfather.

Which of these reasons could explain why there were differences between the two Y chromosomes?

1 Random mutations of certain sections in the Y chromosome could have occurred in his grandfather and father.
2 Pete could have been adopted and not biologically related to his great-grandfather.
3 The Y chromosome of Pete's father sperm underwent independent assortment of homologous chromosomes.
explanation: Random mutations occur in every chromosome including the Y chromosome as they are passed down the generations. This may result in a slight difference in the genetic makeup for the Y chromosome across generations. Pete could also be adopted and inherited a Y chromosome from another person. Since the sperm is a haploid gamete, it does not have homologous chromosomes, thus it is not possible for the sperm to undergo independent assortment of homologous chromosomes.
